h: When Optics is not the right tool
d: Learn what Optics does, what it tests, and the fastest way to see it run.
x: Optics is open-source test automation for apps on Android, iOS, the web and TV. You describe what a person does in your app, such as signing in or adding a product to the cart. Optics repeats it on a real device, an emulator or a browser, and tells you when the app stops behaving. How a test works # A test is a short list of steps in a file, one action per row. A step reads like a sentence: Press Element Sign in , Enter Text email field ava@birch.shop . You don't write code to find things on screen. Optics looks for each element several ways, cheapest first: by its position in the app's UI tree, by its visible text, by reading a screenshot, and by matching a picture of it. When a redesign breaks one way, the next one takes over, so tests break less often. When a run finishes, you get a pass or fail for every step, screenshots of what Optics saw, and a JUnit report that any CI system can read. What you can test # Target How Optics drives it Android and iOS apps Through Appium , on emulators, simulators and real phones Websites Through Playwright or Selenium , no device needed Android TV, Samsung Tizen, LG webOS Through Appium, with the remote's arrow keys. See TV Locked-down production devices As a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen. See Production devices Optics runs on macOS, Linux and Windows with Python 3.12 or newer. There is no account, cloud service or API key. Everything runs on your machine or in your CI. When Optics is not the right tool # Optics tests what a person does through the interface. Reach for something else for unit tests, load testing, API-only contract tests, or pixel-by-pixel visual comparison. d: Install Optics and run a working test in a browser in about five minutes.
x: You'll install Optics, let it create a small project from a working sample, and run that project in a browser. You don't need a phone or an emulator for this. 1 Install Optics # Run the installer for your system. It puts Optics in its own folder ( ~/.optics ), so it doesn't touch the rest of your Python setup. You need Python 3.12 or newer. $ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh PS> irm https://optics-framework.org/install.ps1 | iex $ pip install optics-framework Open a new terminal window, then check that the optics command works: $ optics --version Optics Framework 1.10.5 2 Create a project # Run the guided setup: $ optics quickstart It asks a few questions. Every question has a default, shown in brackets. For this quickstart, answer like this: Question Answer What do you want to automate? web Install Playwright, Selenium now? Yes Start from the 'playwright' example? Yes Project name Press Enter to keep my-optics-project Where should the project live? Press Enter for the current folder Overwrite the template's config.yaml with your own answers? No Optics installs the browser engine, copies the sample into my-optics-project , and checks your setup. Rows marked ⚠️ in that check are optional extras you can add later. 3 Run the test # When Optics asks Run your first test now? , answer yes. You can also run it yourself at any time: $ optics execute my-optics-project A browser window opens, visits a page, checks some text on it and closes. The terminal shows each step as it runs: Test Suite ├── Playwright Suite Setup | 3.54s | PASS │ └── Open Example Page | 3.54s | PASS │ └── Launch App (https://example.com) | 3.54s | PASS ├── TC1 Verify Landing | 0.11s | PASS │ └── Verify Example Page | 0.11s | PASS │ └── Validate Element (text=This domain is for…) | 0.11s | PASS └── Playwright Suite Teardown | 0.12s | PASS └── Close Browser | 0.12s | PASS └── Close And Terminate App | 0.12s | PASS ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed : 3 | Failed: 0 │ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ TC1 Verify Landing fails on Optics 1.10.5 The example page changed its wording after 1.10.5 shipped, so the sample looks for text that is no longer there. Open my-optics-project/test_data/elements.csv and replace its second line with: test_data/elements.csv Heading , text=This domain is for use in documentation examples Then run optics execute my-optics-project again. The next release ships the corrected sample. d: Install the optics command, then add only the drivers and engines your platform needs.
x: Optics has two parts. The core is the optics command, which reads your tests and runs them. Engines are optional add-ons: a driver for each kind of target (browser, phone, TV) and extra ways to find things on screen. You install the core once and add engines as you need them. Before you begin # You need Python 3.12 or newer . Check with: $ python3 --version Python 3.12.13 If you have an older version, install a current one from python.org or your system's package manager. Install the core # We recommend the installer. It creates a private Python environment under ~/.optics , adds optics to your PATH, and leaves your system Python alone. $ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh PS> irm https://optics-framework.org/install.ps1 | iex Use pip when you manage your own virtual environment, for example inside a CI job or an existing test repository. $ python3 -m venv .venv $ source .venv/bin/activate $ pip install optics-framework Open a new terminal so it picks up the updated PATH, then check the install: $ optics --version Optics Framework 1.10.5 Installer options Pass options after sh -s -- . On Windows, set the matching environment variable before running the installer. Option Windows variable What it does --version 1.10.5 OPTICS_VERSION Install a specific release. --extra appium,easyocr OPTICS_EXTRA Install engines at the same time. --dir PATH OPTICS_INSTALL_DIR Install somewhere other than ~/.optics . --no-modify-path OPTICS_NO_MODIFY_PATH Don't edit your shell profile. --dry-run Print what would happen and change nothing. --uninstall Remove the managed install. $ curl -fsSL https://optics-framework.org/install | sh -s -- --extra playwright,easyocr Add engines for your platform # The core install ships without drivers, so it stays small. Add the ones for what you test. optics setup installs engines that match your Optics version: $ optics setup --install playwright Playwright needs no server. Optics downloads its Chromium browser for you. To use Selenium instead, see Web . $ optics setup --install appium You also need the Appium server, the Android SDK (for adb ) and a device or emulator. Set up Android testing covers each one. $ optics setup --install appium You also need the Appium server with the XCUITest driver, Xcode, and a simulator or device. See iOS . Run optics setup with no options to pick engines from a list instead, or optics setup --list to see every name. Optional engines # Add these when a page tells you to. You don't need them for your first test. Engine Install name Adds EasyOCR easyocr Finds elements by reading text on a screenshot. Runs locally. Tesseract pytesseract A lighter OCR engine. Needs the Tesseract program installed too. Google Vision google-vision Cloud OCR. Needs Google Cloud credentials. Gemini llm Plain-English test creation and AI self-heal. Needs a Gemini API key. MCP server mcp Lets AI agents drive Optics. Install with pip: pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" . Bundles install several at once: mobile (Appium), web (Playwright and Selenium), vision (all OCR engines) and all (everything except the MCP server). The engines reference lists every engine. Check your setup # optics doctor checks Python, each engine, and the tools around them: $ optics doctor 🩺 optics doctor Core ✅ python 3.12.13 ✅ optics-framework installed, version 1.10.5 Engines ⚠️ Appium appium-python-client not installed → optics setup --install appium ✅ Playwright playwright 1.63.0 Web ✅ playwright browser Chromium download found ✅ rows are ready. ⚠️ rows are optional or not needed for your platform. Pass a project folder ( optics doctor my_project ) to also check its config.yaml . If the install doesn't work # ** optics: command not found .** Open a new terminal. If it still fails, add ~/.optics/bin to your PATH, as the installer printed. ** optics setup refuses to install.** Conda, pipx and tool-managed environments (uv tool, Poetry, PDM) manage their own packages, so optics setup prints the right command for t

d: Build a test from scratch that signs in to an online store and adds a product to the cart.
x: You'll write a complete test by hand: open a store, sign in, add a backpack to the cart, and check that it worked. Along the way you'll meet the four files every Optics project uses, and see what happens when a test fails. The test runs in a browser against Sauce Labs' demo store , a public site built for practising test automation. You don't need a phone, an emulator or an account. Before you begin Install Optics and the Playwright engine. If you ran the quickstart , you already have both. $ optics setup --install playwright 1 Create an empty project # $ optics init first-test Optics asks which template to start from. Type 1 for (Blank project) and press Enter. You get a folder with empty files and headers already in place: first-test/ ├── config.yaml ├── test_cases/test_cases.csv ├── modules/modules.csv └── test_data/elements.csv The folder names are only a convention. Optics recognises each file by the column names in its first row, so you can move files around later. 2 Tell Optics to use a browser # config.yaml says what Optics drives. Replace its contents with this: config.yaml "c-mod" >driver_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >playwright "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >playwright_find_element "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true - "c-mod" >playwright_page_source "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true - "c-mod" >playwright_screenshot "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >log_level "c-dim" >: WARNING driver_sources picks the browser driver. elements_sources lists the ways Optics may look at the page: asking the browser directly, reading the page's HTML, and taking screenshots. log_level: WARNING keeps the terminal quiet so you can read the results. 3 Name the things you'll touch # Before writing steps, give each field and button a name. Open test_data/elements.csv and add four rows under the header: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID username_field , //input[@id='user-name'] password_field , //input[@id='password'] login_button , //input[@id='login-button'] backpack_add_button , //button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack'] The left column is the name you'll use in steps. The right column tells Optics how to find it. These are XPaths : paths into the page's structure. //input[@id='user-name'] means "the input whose id is user-name ". Finding an element's id Open the store in Chrome, right-click a field and choose Inspect . The highlighted HTML shows the element's id . You don't always need XPaths: Define elements shows how to use visible text and pictures instead. 4 Write the steps # Steps live in modules : small, reusable groups of actions. Open modules/modules.csv and add three modules: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Open the store , Launch App , https://www.saucedemo.com Sign in , Enter Text , ${username_field} , standard_user Sign in , Enter Text , ${password_field} , secret_sauce Sign in , Press Element , ${login_button} Sign in , Assert Presence , Products Add the backpack to the cart , Press Element , ${backpack_add_button} Add the backpack to the cart , Assert Presence , Remove Read each row left to right: the module it belongs to, a keyword (the action), then the values the keyword needs. ${username_field} refers to the name you defined in the previous step. Products and Remove are plain text that should appear on screen: the products page title, and the label the backpack's button changes to once it's in the cart. Enter Text fails in browsers on Optics 1.10.5 On 1.10.5, every Enter Text in a browser fails with Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable . A fix is on its way in the next release. Until you upgrade, click the field and type into it in two steps. Replace the two Enter Text rows with these four: modules/modules.csv Sign in , Press Element , ${username_field} Sign in , Enter Text Direct , standard_user Sign in , Press Element , ${password_field} Sign in , Enter Text Direct ,

d: Learn the five ideas every Optics test is built from, and what happens when a test runs.
x: An Optics test is data, not code. You write down what a person does in plain rows. Optics works out how to do each step on the screen in front of it. Keywords # A keyword is one action or check, such as Press Element , Enter Text or Assert Presence . Every step in a test is one keyword plus the values it needs. Keywords fall into four groups: Group Use it to Examples App management Open and close the app or website Launch App , Close And Terminate App Actions Tap, type, swipe and press keys Press Element , Enter Text , Scroll Verification Check what's on screen Assert Presence , Validate Element Flow control Repeat steps, branch, read data, call APIs Run Loop , Condition , Read Data The same keywords work on every platform. Press Element taps on a phone and clicks in a browser. The keyword reference lists all of them, and optics list prints them in your terminal. Elements # An element is a name for something on screen, like sign_in or search_bar . Steps use the name inside ${…} , and elements.csv says how to find it: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //*[@resource-id='login'] sign_in , Sign in search_bar , //*[@resource-id='search'] Keeping locators in one file means a redesign is a one-line change, not an edit to every test. An element can have several values. sign_in above can be found by its id or by its text, and Optics tries them in order until one works. A value can be an XPath (a path through the app's UI tree), visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. Elements can also hold plain data, such as a username, so one file holds everything a test might change. Modules # A module is a named, reusable sequence of steps, like Sign In or Add To Cart . Write a flow once as a module and reuse it in as many test cases as you like. When the sign-in screen changes, you fix one module. Test cases # A test case is a flow you want to check, made of modules in order. Checkout might run Sign In , Add To Cart and Pay . Each test case passes or fails on its own. Two names are special. A test case called Suite Setup runs before all the others, and Suite Teardown runs after them. Use them to launch the app once and close it at the end. Configuration # config.yaml says what Optics drives and how it may look at the screen. It holds lists of engines : A driver controls the target: Appium for phones and TVs, Playwright or Selenium for browsers, or a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse for locked-down devices. Element sources are ways to look at the screen: ask the app directly, read its UI tree, or take a screenshot. Text detection (OCR) and image detection are optional. They let Optics find elements on a screenshot when the UI tree can't help. The tests themselves never mention engines. That's why the same test runs on a phone today and against a different device tomorrow. What happens during a run # When you run optics execute , Optics: Reads every file in the project folder and decides what each one is from its column names. Runs Suite Setup , then each test case in order, then Suite Teardown . For each step, takes a screenshot, finds the element, and performs the action. If a step fails, skips the rest of that test case and moves on to the next one. One broken flow doesn't stop the run. At the end, checks the last screen for known error messages, if you've defined any . Writes the results to execution_output/ , and exits with 0 if every test case passed or 1 if any failed. How Optics finds an element # For each value of an element, Optics tries the cheapest ways first. An XPath is looked up in the UI tree. Text is looked up in the UI tree, and if it isn't there, Optics reads a screenshot with OCR. A picture is matched against a screenshot. If everything fails and you've switched on AI self-heal , an AI model looks at the screen and tries to recover. How Optics finds elements covers the full order and how to tune it. h: Every way ends in plain text
d: Learn which way of creating tests fits your team. Every way produces the same files.
x: Optics gives you several ways to turn a user flow into a test. They all end in the same plain-text suite: CSV or YAML files that live in your repository and run with optics execute . You can mix them in one project, so a test someone recorded can sit next to one an AI agent wrote. Choose your approach # Write it No code List the steps in a spreadsheet or text editor. Anyone can read and review them. Record it No code Run steps one at a time against the live app in optics live . What works is saved. Describe it AI Type what you want in plain English. An AI model drives the app and keeps the steps. Delegate it AI Connect your AI agent with optics mcp . It explores the app and writes the suite. Code it in Python Code Call keywords from pytest or any Python script. Code it in Robot Framework Code Use Optics keywords in .robot files. Which one should I use? # We recommend recording for most people starting out. You see each step work on the real app before it's saved, and you end up with readable CSV files you can edit by hand later. Teams then usually write small changes directly in the files. Choose describe or delegate when you have a Gemini API key or an AI agent, and want a first draft of a long flow quickly. Review what the AI saved, the same way you'd review a colleague's change. Choose Python or Robot Framework only if your tests need logic that the files can't express, or your team already runs everything through pytest or Robot. Code-based tests lose the main benefit of Optics files: that anyone on the team can read them. d: Write test cases, modules and elements by hand, in CSV or YAML.
x: Writing a suite by hand is the most direct way to create tests, and it's how most edits happen once a suite exists. You need a text editor or a spreadsheet app. This page covers the three files a suite is made of, in the order we recommend writing them. Set up a project # Create a project with optics init , then fill in its files: $ optics init birch-tests Pick (Blank project) when asked for a template. You get this layout: birch-tests/ ├── config.yaml # what to drive ├── test_cases/test_cases.csv # which flows run ├── modules/modules.csv # the steps └── test_data/elements.csv # names for things on screen Optics finds each file by what's inside it, not by its name or folder. A CSV whose first row is test_case,test_step is a test-cases file wherever it sits. You can split a big suite across several files of each kind. If you haven't set up config.yaml yet, Install Optics and the platform guides show what to put in it. Choose CSV or YAML # Both formats load into the same suite, and one project can hold both. Pick the one your team reads best: CSV opens in any spreadsheet. Each step is one row, so a diff shows exactly which step changed. YAML keeps a whole flow in one indented file, which reads well in a code editor. The examples on this page show both. Choose a tab and the rest of the page follows. Write tests in YAML covers the YAML rules in detail. Name the things on screen # Start with elements : a name for each field, button or label your test touches, and how to find it. test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID email_field , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email'] password_field , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password'] sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] sign_in , Sign in search_bar , Search Birch password , correct-horse birch.yaml "c-mod" >Elements "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >email_field "c-dim" >: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']" "c-mod" >password_field "c-dim" >: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']" "c-mod" >sign_in "c-dim" >: [ "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']" , "Sign in" ] "c-mod" >search_bar "c-dim" >: Search Birch "c-mod" >password "c-dim" >: correct-horse The header must be exactly Element_Name,Element_ID . Repeat a name, or give a list in YAML, to add fallbacks : Optics tries the values in order until one works. Here sign_in is found by its id, or by its text if the id changes. A value can be an XPath, visible text, or the file name of a picture of the element. Define elements explains each kind and when to use it. Tip Elements can hold test data too, such as email,ava@birch.shop . Keeping data next to locators means one file holds everything that changes between environments. Write the steps as modules # A module is a named list of steps. Each step is one keyword and its values. modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Launch Birch , Launch App Sign In , Enter Text , ${email_field} , ava@birch.shop Sign In , Enter Text , ${password_field} , ${password} Sign In , Press Element , ${sign_in} Sign In , Assert Presence , Picked for you Add To Cart , Press Element , ${search_bar} Add To Cart , Enter Text Direct , trail runner Add To Cart , Press Element , Trail Runner 2 Add To Cart , Press Element , Add to cart Add To Cart , Assert Presence , Added to cart birch.yaml "c-mod" >Modules "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >Launch Birch "c-dim" >: - Launch App - "c-mod" >Sign In "c-dim" >: - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password} - Press Element ${sign_in} - Assert Presence "Picked for you" - "c-mod" >Add To Cart "c-dim" >: - Press Element ${search_bar} - Enter Text Direct "trail runner" - Press Element "Trail Runner 2" - Press Element "Add to cart" - Assert Presence "Added to cart" How a step is read: Keyword names are case-insensitive. d: Build a test by running steps one at a time against the live app, then save the ones that worked.
x: optics live opens an interactive session next to your device or browser. You type a step, Optics runs it straight away, and you see whether it worked. Every step that succeeds is recorded. When the flow is done, /save writes it into your suite as a module, ready for optics execute . Before you begin # You need a project with a working config.yaml that has exactly one driver enabled. Any project from optics quickstart or the first test tutorial works. For a phone, start the Appium server and your emulator first. See Android or iOS . Start a session # $ optics live birch-tests Leave out the folder to use the current one. Optics opens the app straight away (it runs launch_app for you), so the first line of the session is already a recorded step. The screen has three parts: ✓ launch_app 1.21s ✓ enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop 0.48s [XPath] ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── › press_element "Sign in" ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── appium:emulator-5554 · rec ● · /help · /quit · Tab complete · Ctrl-K keywords · Ctrl-N AI mode History , at the top: each step with ✓ or ✗, how long it took, and how the element was found ( [XPath] , [Text] , [OCR] or [Image] ). Input , in the middle: where you type. Status bar , at the bottom: the device or browser you're connected to, and rec ● to show recording is on. Run steps # Type a keyword and its values, separated by spaces, and press Enter : › enter_text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop › enter_text ${password_field} "correct horse" › press_element "Sign in" › assert_presence "Picked for you" Write keyword names in snake_case or in words: press_element , Press Element and press element all work. Put quotes around a value that contains spaces. Type ${ to pick from the elements already defined in your project. Press Tab to complete a keyword name. The rest of its parameters appear in grey as a hint. Press Ctrl + K to browse every keyword. If a step fails, it's shown with ✗ and the reason, and it isn't recorded. Try a different value and run it again. Only steps that work end up in your test. Save the recording # When the flow works, save it with a test case name and a module name: › /save Checkout Sign_In • Saved 4 step(s) → module 'Sign_In' in modules/modules.csv, test case 'Checkout' in test_cases/test_cases.csv Optics then: appends the steps to modules/modules.csv as the module Sign_In , adds a Checkout,Sign_In row to test_cases/test_cases.csv , copies the session's screenshots to execution_output/Sign_In/ , clears the recording, so the next steps you run become the next module. Run more steps, then /save Checkout Add_To_Cart to add a second module to the same test case. Note Names in /save can't contain spaces. Use underscores, or rename the module in modules.csv afterwards. If the module or test case already exists, Optics asks you to run the same /save again to confirm that you want to append to it. /save writes the steps exactly as you typed them. If you typed press_element "Sign in" , the module uses the text Sign in . To use a named element instead, type ${sign_in} , or edit modules.csv afterwards and add the element to elements.csv . /save always writes CSV, even in a project that uses YAML. Commands and keys # Command What it does /save <test_case> <module> Save the recorded steps as a module in a test case. /elements Show every element defined in the project. /screenshot Save a screenshot to screenshots/ . /device Pick a different connected phone or emulator (Appium only). /device <id> switches directly. /help Show help. /quit Leave. If you have unsaved steps, Optics warns you once; /quit again discards them. Key What it does Enter Run the step. Tab / Shift + Tab Complete a keyword or element name. ↑ / ↓ Recall earlier input. Ctrl + K Browse keywords. Ctrl + N Switch to plain-English mode. See Describe a test . Ctrl + X Stop a plain-English run. Esc Close a popup. Ctrl + C or Ctrl + D Quit. On Android, plugging in

t: Describe a test in plain English
h: Write goals the model can finish
d: Tell Optics what to do in a sentence, let an AI model drive the app, and keep the steps it took.
x: In plain-English mode, you type a goal like add trail runners to the cart . An AI model looks at the screen, picks one keyword at a time, and runs it on the real device until the goal is done. The steps it took are recorded like any other optics live steps, and /save writes them into your suite. This mode uses Google's Gemini models. It's the fastest way to draft a long flow, and the result is ordinary keywords you can read and edit. Before you begin # You need: A project that works in optics live . A Gemini API key from Google AI Studio , or a Google Cloud project with Vertex AI. 1 Install the AI engine # $ optics setup --install llm 2 Turn it on in config.yaml # Add an llm_models section to your project's config.yaml : config.yaml "c-mod" >llm_models "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >gemini "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >model "c-dim" >: gemini-2.5-flash model is optional; gemini-2.5-flash is the default. 3 Give Optics your key # Set the key as an environment variable in the terminal you'll run optics live from: $ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key" PS> $env:GEMINI_API_KEY = "your-key" Warning Don't put API keys in config.yaml . The file is meant to be committed with your tests, and a key in it would be shared with everyone who can read the repository. To use Vertex AI instead, set GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI=true , GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT and GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION , and sign in with your usual Google Cloud credentials. Describe a flow # Start optics live , then press Ctrl + N . The prompt changes from › to ai › . Type what you want in plain English: ai › add trail runners to the cart ⋯ [ai] add trail runners to the cart thinking: open search and look for the shoes ✓ press_element "Search Birch" 0.42s [Text] ✓ enter_text "Search Birch" "trail runner" 0.51s [Text] thinking: Trail Runner 2 is the first result ✓ press_element "Trail Runner 2" 0.88s [OCR] ✓ press_element "Add to cart" 0.37s [Text] ✓ [ai] add trail runners to the cart done · 4 step(s) · 9.4s · recorded 4 (/save to keep) Each turn, the model sees a screenshot, the list of elements on screen, your project's element names and the steps so far. Its reasoning appears as thinking: lines. Every action is a normal keyword, so it uses the same ways of finding elements as a test you wrote yourself. Press Ctrl + X to stop a run, or Ctrl + N again to go back to typing keywords. You can mix both modes in one session. Keep the steps # When the goal is reached, Optics asks the model to drop dead ends and detours, so the recording keeps only the steps that mattered. If it pruned anything, the summary says so, for example (kept 4 of 6 steps) . Save the steps the same way as a manual recording: ai › /save Checkout Add_To_Cart Only runs that finish successfully are recorded. If the model gives up, hits its step limit, or you stop it, nothing from that run is saved. Review what you saved # Open modules/modules.csv and read the new rows before you commit them. The model names elements by their visible text, such as "Add to cart" . For steps that matter, replace the text with a named element from elements.csv and add a fallback, as described in Define elements . Write goals the model can finish # Describe one outcome per instruction. Sign in as ava@birch.shop works better than a whole checkout in one sentence. Run several instructions in a row instead. Use the words on screen. Tap Add to cart is clearer than buy it . Give values explicitly. Search for "trail runner" , not search for shoes . Each run stops after 15 steps, after 3 failed steps in a row, or when the model repeats gestures without getting closer. Break long flows into smaller goals. Limits # Gemini is the only supported model provider. Each step is a call to the model, so a run costs API usage and takes several seconds per step. Screenshots go to Google's API while the mode is on. Don't use it on screens that show data you can't send to a third party. See also # Record a test AI self-hea

t: Let your AI agent build tests
d: Connect Optics to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client so your agent can drive a device and write the suite.
x: optics mcp is a Model Context Protocol server. It gives an AI agent eyes and hands on a phone, TV or browser: every Optics keyword becomes a tool the agent can call, and the screen becomes something it can read. The agent explores your app, then writes an ordinary Optics suite that you review and run with optics execute . The agent is yours. Optics doesn't call any AI service in this mode, so it works with whichever model your client uses. Before you begin # An MCP client, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor or VS Code. A target to drive: a browser (Playwright needs nothing else), or a phone or emulator with an Appium server running. See Platforms . 1 Install the MCP server # The MCP server is a separate extra. Install it with pip, in the same environment as Optics: $ pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" If you used the installer, run ~/.optics/venv/bin/pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" instead. 2 Add Optics to your client # $ claude mcp add optics -- optics mcp Add this to claude_desktop_config.json ( Settings → Developer → Edit config ), then restart Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } Add this to .cursor/mcp.json in your project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for every project: .cursor/mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } Add this to .vscode/mcp.json : .vscode/mcp.json { "servers" : { "optics" : { "type" : "stdio" , "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } If your client can't find optics , use its full path, for example ~/.optics/bin/optics . 3 Ask for a test # Describe the flow and where the app runs. The agent starts a session, explores, and writes files: Use the optics tools to open https://www.saucedemo.com in Playwright. Sign in as standard_user / secret_sauce, add the backpack to the cart, and check that the cart badge shows 1. Then write it as an Optics suite in ./checkout, run optics dry_run on it, and tell me how to run it. For a phone app, include the Appium details: start an appium session at http://127.0.0.1:4723 with platformName Android, deviceName emulator-5554, appPackage com.birch.shop . 4 Review and run the suite # The agent writes the same files you would: test cases, modules and elements, in CSV. Read them like a colleague's pull request, then run them: $ optics execute checkout What the agent can do # The server gives the agent: Session tools : start_session (picks the driver, URL and device settings, and opens the app), screenshot and terminate_session . A tool for each keyword , such as press_element , enter_text , assert_presence and launch_app . Each takes the session id plus the keyword's values. Resources to read : the current screen as an image, the list of elements on screen, the raw UI tree, the keyword catalogue, and optics://project-format , which teaches the agent how to write suite files. A typical session goes: start a session, look at the screen, act with keywords, read the project format, write the files, run optics dry_run , and end the session. The MCP reference lists every tool and resource. Keep the agent on track # Agents tap by name, not by position. Tapping raw screen coordinates is hidden by default, because those tests break on any other screen size. Set OPTICS_MCP_ALLOW_COORDINATE_TAPS=1 before starting the server if you really need it. Saving is the agent's job. There's no record button in MCP. The agent writes the files using optics://project-format . Ask it to run optics dry_run before it finishes. Loops and conditions ( Run Loop , Condition , Read Data and the rest) aren't tools, because they only make sense inside suite files. The agent can still write them into modules. Sessions are private to the server. A session started over MCP isn't visible to optics serve or optics live , and it ends when the server stops. h: How calls differ from suite files
d: Call Optics keywords from pytest or any Python script when a test needs real code.
x: Every keyword is also a method on the Optics class. Use it when a test needs logic the suite files can't express, or when your team already runs everything through pytest. You keep the same fallbacks, OCR and image matching as a CSV suite. Note If CSV or YAML files can express your test, prefer them. Anyone on the team can read and review a suite file, and the runner gives you the step tree, screenshots and error detection for free. See Choose how to create tests . Write a test with pytest # This test signs in to the Sauce Labs demo store, adds a backpack to the cart, and reads the cart badge. It runs as written with pip install "optics-framework[playwright]" pytest . test_checkout.py import pytest from optics_framework import Optics CONFIG = { "driver_sources" : [{ "playwright" : { "enabled" : True }}], "elements_sources" : [ { "playwright_find_element" : { "enabled" : True }}, { "playwright_page_source" : { "enabled" : True }}, { "playwright_screenshot" : { "enabled" : True }}, ], } @pytest.fixture def optics(): with Optics(CONFIG) as session: # quits the browser when the test ends yield session def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics): optics.launch_app( "https://www.saucedemo.com" ) optics.enter_text( "//input[@id='user-name']" , "standard_user" ) optics.enter_text( "//input[@id='password']" , "secret_sauce" ) optics.press_element([ "//input[@id='login-button']" , "Login" ]) # fallbacks optics.assert_presence( "Products" , timeout= "10" ) optics.press_element( "//button[@id='add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack']" ) badge = optics.get_text( "//span[@data-test='shopping-cart-badge']" ) assert badge == "1" $ pytest test_checkout.py Typing and reading text in browsers on Optics 1.10.5 On 1.10.5, enter_text and get_text fail with Playwright ( Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable ). The next release fixes it. Until then, click the field with press_element and type with enter_text_direct . Configure the session # Pass the same lists you'd put in config.yaml , as a Python dict. driver_sources and elements_sources are required. The SDK reads these keys: Key What it's for driver_sources , elements_sources What to drive and how to look at the screen. See the config reference . text_detection , image_detection OCR and image matching engines, if you use them. project_path A folder to search for image files and to resolve relative paths in read_data . Required for image elements. execution_output_path Where screenshots and results go. To reuse a project's config.yaml , load it yourself and pass the dict: import yaml from optics_framework import Optics with open( "birch-tests/config.yaml" ) as f: config = yaml.safe_load(f) config[ "project_path" ] = "birch-tests" with Optics(config) as optics: optics.launch_app() Settings such as ai_self_heal , llm_models and log_level aren't read by the SDK. How calls differ from suite files # Method names are snake_case. Press Element is press_element . Your editor's autocomplete lists them all. Pass every value as a string. optics.press_by_coordinates("540", "1600") works; numbers raise TypeError . A list means "try these in order". press_element(["//button[@id='login']", "Login"]) tries the XPath, then the text. To check several elements at once, separate them with a pipe in one string: assert_presence("Products|Your Cart") . ** ${name} isn't looked up** in action methods. Pass the locator itself, or keep your own dict of locators. Methods return values. get_text returns the text, capture_screenshot returns a base64 PNG, and assert_presence returns True . A failed check raises an exception, which fails the pytest test. Some defaults differ. assert_presence and assert_visibility wait 60 seconds by default, and detect_and_press waits 10. Python-only methods # These have no CSV equivalent: Method What it does add_element(name, value) Add a value to a named element, for use in flow-control methods. get_element_value(name) Return the list of values for a named element. add_module(name, steps) De

h: How Optics keywords behave in Robot
Generate Robot code from a suite
d: Import Optics as a Robot Framework library and use its keywords in .robot files.
x: Optics is also a Robot Framework library. If your team already writes .robot suites, you can add Optics keywords to them and get its fallbacks, OCR and image matching without changing tools. Before you begin # Robot Framework isn't installed with Optics. Add it to the same environment: $ pip install robotframework "optics-framework[appium]" Swap appium for the engine you use. You also need a config.yaml with driver_sources and elements_sources . Any Optics project's config works. Write a suite # checkout.robot *** Settings *** Library OperatingSystem Library optics_framework.optics.Optics Suite Setup Open Optics Suite Teardown Quit *** Variables *** ${EMAIL_FIELD} //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/email"] *** Keywords *** Open Optics ${config} = Get File ${CURDIR} /config.yaml Setup config= ${config} *** Test Cases *** Shopper Can Sign In Launch App Detect And Press Allow timeout=5 Enter Text ${EMAIL_FIELD} ava@birch.shop ${sign_in} = Create List //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/login"] Sign in Press Element ${sign_in} Assert Presence Picked for you|Search Birch timeout=20 rule=any Run it like any Robot suite: $ robot checkout.robot How Optics keywords behave in Robot # Setup takes the config's contents, not its path. Read the file with Get File as shown above, then pass the text to Setup . If you use image elements, add project_path: . to the config so Optics can find the pictures. Pass fallbacks as a list. Create List builds the values to try in order. Writing several plain arguments fills the keyword's next parameters instead. Separate several elements with a pipe inside one argument: Picked for you|Search Birch . Named arguments use the Python names : timeout=20 , rule=any , index=1 . **Robot replaces ${…} itself.** To pass an Optics variable to Evaluate or Condition , escape it: \${total} . ** Sleep and Evaluate exist in Robot's BuiltIn library too.** Robot warns and uses the Optics version, which only accepts whole seconds. Write BuiltIn.Sleep 2s or Optics.Sleep 2 to be explicit. The keyword reference lists every keyword. The Python-only keywords in Use Optics from Python , such as Add Element and Add Module , work in Robot too. Generate Robot code from a suite # If you already have a CSV or YAML suite, optics generate can write a starting .robot file from it. See Generate pytest or Robot code . See also # Use Optics from Python config.yaml reference

h: Open and close the app once
Run the same suite on different devices
Name things so failures explain themselves
d: Structure a growing suite with setup and teardown, shared modules, several files and run selection.
x: A handful of tests fits in three files. A suite that covers a whole app needs a little structure so changes stay small. This page covers the tools Optics gives you for that. Open and close the app once # Name a test case Suite Setup and it runs once, before every other test case. Suite Teardown runs once at the end. Use them to launch and close the app, so each test case can focus on its own flow: test_cases/test_cases.csv test_case,test_step Suite Setup , Launch Birch Shopper can sign in , Sign In Shopper can search , Sign In Shopper can search , Search For Shoes Suite Teardown , Close Birch modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Launch Birch , Launch App Close Birch , Close And Terminate App Optics matches these names loosely: any test case name containing both "suite" and "setup" counts, so Birch Suite Setup works too. Setup and teardown always run, even when you select which tests run . Per-test Setup and Teardown Test cases named just Setup or Teardown are meant to run around every test case. In Optics 1.10.5 they only wrap the first test case, so don't rely on them yet. Put shared steps in a module and list it at the start of each test case instead, as Sign In is above. Avoid "setup" and "teardown" in ordinary test names for the same reason: a test called Setup wizard works is treated as the per-test setup. Reuse modules # A module can appear in as many test cases as you like. Keep each module small and focused on one screen or one task, such as Sign In , Search For Shoes or Open Cart . When that screen changes, you fix one module and every test that uses it follows. To call one module from inside another, use Execute Module : modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Buy Trail Runners , Execute Module , Search For Shoes Buy Trail Runners , Press Element , Trail Runner 2 Buy Trail Runners , Press Element , Add to cart Listing a module's name as a step on its own doesn't work; you need Execute Module . Steps inside a module called this way use only the first value of each element, so give important elements a value that's reliable on its own. Conditions and loops explains the details. Split a suite across files # Optics reads every CSV and YAML file in the project folder and its subfolders, and recognises each by its first row (or top-level key in YAML). So you can split a large suite however suits your team: birch-tests/ ├── config.yaml ├── checkout/ │ ├── test_cases.csv │ └── modules.csv ├── search/ │ ├── test_cases.csv │ └── modules.csv └── elements/ ├── shared.csv └── checkout.csv When two files define the same thing: Elements with the same name are merged, and every value becomes a fallback. Modules and test cases with the same name: the one read last wins, and Optics logs a warning. Keep names unique. Tip Optics also reads files inside execution_output/ . Keep stray CSV or YAML files, and copies of old suites, out of the project folder so they don't get picked up. Run only some test cases # There's no command-line flag for this. List the test cases to run, or to skip, in config.yaml : config.yaml "c-mod" >include "c-dim" >: - Shopper can sign in - Shopper can search config.yaml "c-mod" >exclude "c-dim" >: - Shopper can pay with a gift card Names match exactly, ignoring case. Use include or exclude , not both. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run. Run the same suite on different devices # Keep one config file in a project. Optics uses the config it finds in the project folder, so two of them would compete. To run the same suite on several targets, keep one config per target outside the project and copy the one you need into place before the run: birch/ ├── configs/ │ ├── pixel-8.yaml │ └── chrome.yaml └── birch-tests/ ├── config.yaml # copied from configs/ before each run └── … $ cp configs/pixel-8.yaml birch-tests/config.yaml $ optics execute birch-tests Name things so failures explain themselves # The run's tree and the JUnit report use your names, so a good name saves a trip into the fi

h: A complete suite in one file
d: Keep a whole flow in one indented file, and learn the quoting rules that make YAML steps work.
x: YAML suites hold the same test cases, modules and elements as CSV, in one file you can read top to bottom. Optics loads both formats into the same suite, so a project can mix them. A complete suite in one file # checkout.yaml "c-mod" >Test Cases "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >Suite Setup "c-dim" >: - Launch Birch - "c-mod" >Shopper can add trail runners "c-dim" >: - Sign In - Add To Cart "c-mod" >Modules "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >Launch Birch "c-dim" >: - Launch App - "c-mod" >Sign In "c-dim" >: - Enter Text ${email_field} ava@birch.shop - Enter Text ${password_field} ${password} - Press Element ${sign_in} - Assert Presence "Picked for you" - "c-mod" >Add To Cart "c-dim" >: - Press Element "Trail Runner 2" - Press Element "Add to cart" - Assert Presence "Added to cart" timeout_str=10 "c-mod" >Elements "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >email_field "c-dim" >: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/email']" "c-mod" >password_field "c-dim" >: "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/password']" "c-mod" >sign_in "c-dim" >: - "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']" - Sign in "c-mod" >password "c-dim" >: correct-horse Keep config.yaml as its own file. You can split the suite into several YAML files, or keep elements in CSV and steps in YAML. The rules # Section names are exact # Write the three top-level keys exactly as Test Cases , Modules and Elements , with that capitalization. Other spellings, such as test_cases: , are recognised as a suite file but load nothing, and the run then reports that there are no test cases. Each step is one line # A step is a single string: the keyword name, then its values separated by spaces. Optics matches the longest keyword name it knows at the start of the line, so Press Element Sign in is read as the keyword Press Element with the value Sign , then in as a second value. Quote any value that contains spaces: - Press Element "Sign in" - Enter Text ${email_field} "Ava Birch" A step that is exactly a module name runs that module. Named values # name=value sets one parameter by name, like timeout_str=10 above. Quote the value if it contains spaces: event_name="tap sign in" . Expressions with = in them # Optics splits a quoted value on its first = to support named values. That breaks quoted expressions that contain == . Write such expressions without spaces, and without quotes: # Works - Condition ${status} == 'ready' "Go Home" "Sign In" # Doesn't work: the quotes around the expression are kept - Condition " ${status} == 'ready'" "Go Home" "Sign In" Quoted values without = are fine, such as "Go Home" . Module names as values # When a keyword takes a module name, such as Run Loop or Execute Module , quote names that contain spaces: Run Loop "Search One" term "trail runner|pace knit" . Elements # An element is a single value or a list. A list gives fallbacks, tried in order: "c-mod" >Elements "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >sign_in "c-dim" >: [ "//*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login']" , "Sign in" , sign_in.png] Quote XPaths. They contain characters YAML treats specially, such as [ , @ and : . What stays in CSV # Error definitions are CSV only. See Catch error screens . ** /save in optics live ** always writes CSV, even in a YAML project. Move the steps into your YAML file afterwards, or keep the CSV next to it. See also # Write a test suite , with CSV and YAML side by side Project files reference

h: 1. Each value of the element, in order
2. Each way to find that kind of value
3. Each element source, in config order
d: Learn how Optics tries several ways to find each element, so one changed locator doesn't fail a test.
x: Most test tools give an element one locator, and the test fails the moment that locator changes. Optics assumes an element has several identities (its place in the UI tree, its text, what it looks like) and tries them in order before giving up. A redesign that breaks one identity falls through to the next. The order Optics tries things # When a step needs an element, Optics works through three layers of fallback. 1. Each value of the element, in order # An element can have several values in elements.csv . Optics tries them top to bottom and stops at the first that works: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] sign_in , Sign in sign_in , sign_in.png 2. Each way to find that kind of value # Optics looks at a value and decides what kind it is, then tries the ways that fit, cheapest first: Value looks like Optics tries Needs An XPath, such as //*[@resource-id='login'] The UI tree A driver that exposes a UI tree Text, such as Sign in 1. The UI tree 2. OCR on a screenshot OCR needs a text detection engine An image file, such as sign_in.png Image matching on a screenshot An image detection engine text_only:Sign in OCR only, skipping the UI tree A text detection engine Looking something up in the UI tree takes milliseconds. OCR and image matching read a screenshot, which takes longer, so Optics only uses them when the tree can't help. Define elements shows every kind of value. 3. Each element source, in config order # config.yaml lists element sources : the ways Optics may look at the screen, such as asking the app directly, reading its UI tree, or taking a screenshot. Optics tries them in the order they're listed. If you enable more than one driver, each is tried in turn as well. Last resort: AI self-heal # If everything above fails and you've switched it on, an AI model looks at the screen and tries to finish the step, for example by spotting that Sign in is now Log in . It's off by default. See AI self-heal . See which way worked # Optics records how it found each element, so you can tell when a test is passing on a fallback: optics live shows it after each step: 0.31s [Text] . Screenshots in execution_output/ show a box around the element Optics found, for drivers that report element positions. See Read the results . If a test keeps passing on its second or third value, the first one is probably out of date. Update it while you still know why. Make elements last # Put the most stable value first. An id that developers don't change is better than text that marketing rewrites. Add a text fallback to important buttons. Text survives most layout changes. Use images last. Image matching is the slowest, and a restyled button stops matching. It's still the only option for icons with no text or id. Narrow the search when the same text appears twice on a screen. Use index to pick a match, or an area of interest to look in one part of the screen. See also # Define elements Find elements by text and image Search part of the screen AI self-heal

d: Name the things your tests touch, choose good values for them, and add fallbacks that survive redesigns.
x: An element is a name for something on screen, plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to elements by name ( ${sign_in} ), so when the app changes, you update the element once and every test follows. Write elements # Elements live in any CSV whose header starts with Element_Name,Element_ID . The project template puts them in test_data/elements.csv . test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] sign_in , Sign in cart_icon , cart_icon.png search_bar , Search Birch email , ava@birch.shop To give an element several values, repeat its name on more rows. Optics tries them top to bottom. You can also add more columns whose names start with Element_ID , such as Element_ID_text or Element_ID_image , and fill them in on the same row: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID,Element_ID_text,Element_ID_image sign_in , //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] , Sign in , sign_in.png Both layouts mean the same thing. Use whichever is easier to read for your team. Empty cells are ignored. The header is exact The first column must be named exactly Element_Name , with that capitalization. A file headed element_name,element_id is recognised as an elements file but loads no elements, and every ${name} then fails with "Element not found". Choose the kind of value # Optics decides what a value is from how it looks: Write Optics treats it as Example Starts with / , // or ( XPath, looked up in the UI tree //*[@resource-id='login'] Plain words Text: UI tree first, then OCR on a screenshot Sign in text_only: then words Text, OCR only text_only:Sign in Ends in .png , .jpg , .jpeg or .bmp An image to match on a screenshot cart_icon.png css= , #id , .class or tag[attr] A CSS selector. Works with Playwright, not Selenium #login-button Starts with android. or XCUI A class name android.widget.Switch XPath # An XPath is a path through the app's UI tree. It's the fastest and most precise kind of value, and the best first choice when the app has stable ids: Android: //*[@resource-id='com.birch.shop:id/login'] iOS: //XCUIElementTypeButton[@name='Sign in'] Web: //button[@id='login'] To pick the second of several matches, wrap the XPath in parentheses and add an index: (//android.widget.Button)[2] . Text # Plain text matches an element showing that text, or with that accessibility label. It's the most readable kind of value, and it survives layout changes. If the text isn't in the UI tree, for example because it's drawn inside an image or a game canvas, Optics reads the screenshot with OCR, as long as a text detection engine is enabled. Text matching in the UI tree tolerates small differences. To require exact matches, set strict_element_match: true in config.yaml . Text that looks like something else A value is checked against the rules in the table above, top to bottom. Text that happens to start with ( or / , or contains [ and ] , is read as an XPath or CSS selector: (optional) , Price [USD] , .com . On Appium and Playwright, put text= in front to force text: text=(optional) . Images # An image value is the file name of a cropped picture of the element. Put the picture anywhere in the project folder (the templates use test_data/input_templates/ ) and refer to it by file name only. Image matching is the slowest kind and needs an image detection engine. Use it for icons with no text or id. Find elements by text and image shows how to capture a good picture. Values to avoid # id: values, such as id:login , aren't supported by any element source and always fail. Use an XPath on the id instead. Find the right locator # **In optics live **, try a value with press_element or assert_presence before you write it down. The history line shows whether it worked and how it was found. Android and iOS : Appium Inspector shows each element's id, text and XPath. Web : right-click an element in Chrome and choose Inspect . Any platform : the Get Interactive Elements keyword lists the but

t: Find elements by text and image
h: Enable it, and a screenshot source
d: Use OCR and image matching to find elements the UI tree can't see, such as text inside images, canvases and video.
x: Some things on screen never appear in the app's UI tree: text drawn inside an image, a game or map canvas, a video player's controls, or anything on a device you can only watch through a camera. Optics can find these by looking at a screenshot, the way a person would. It reads text with OCR (optical character recognition) and finds icons with image matching . Both are slower than the UI tree, so Optics only uses them after the faster ways fail. You turn them on in config.yaml . Turn on OCR # 1 Install an OCR engine # We recommend EasyOCR. It runs on your machine and needs no account. $ optics setup --install easyocr The first run downloads EasyOCR's models, which takes a minute. 2 Enable it, and a screenshot source # OCR reads screenshots, so elements_sources must include a screenshot source for your driver ( appium_screenshot , playwright_screenshot , selenium_screenshot , or camera_screenshot ): config.yaml "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >appium_find_element "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true - "c-mod" >appium_page_source "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true - "c-mod" >appium_screenshot "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >text_detection "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >easyocr "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true 3 Use text values # Nothing changes in your tests. Any text value, such as Press Element,Trail Runner 2 , is tried in the UI tree first and with OCR second. To skip the UI tree and use OCR straight away, write text_only:Trail Runner 2 . OCR engines # Engine Name in config Install Good to know EasyOCR easyocr optics setup --install easyocr Local and accurate. Slower on the first call while models load. Reads English. Tesseract pytesseract optics setup --install pytesseract , plus the Tesseract program Light and fast. Matches whole words exactly. Google Cloud Vision google_vision optics setup --install google-vision Cloud service. Set GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS to a service account key. Screenshots leave your machine. Your own service remote_ocr Nothing Sends screenshots to a URL you run. See the engines reference . List more than one engine and Optics tries them in order. Turn on image matching # Image matching finds a picture of an element, such as an icon, on the screen. It needs no extra install. config.yaml "c-mod" >image_detection "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >templatematch "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true Then use the picture's file name as an element value: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID cart_icon , //*[@content-desc='Cart'] cart_icon , cart_icon.png Capture a good template # The picture is called a template . How you crop it decides whether matching works: Take a screenshot on the same kind of device you test on. Run the test once and use a pre_… screenshot from execution_output/ , or run /screenshot in optics live . Crop tightly around the element. Include its distinctive shape, and as little background as possible. Don't resize the crop. Matching works best at the screen's own resolution, though it tolerates some scaling and rotation. Save it as PNG anywhere in the project folder. The templates use test_data/input_templates/ . Refer to it by file name only: cart_icon.png , not a path. File names must be unique across the project. Optics also picks up images inside execution_output/ . Give templates distinctive names, so they never clash with a screenshot's name. When to use which # Situation Use The element has a stable id or text in the UI tree XPath or text, no vision needed Text drawn inside an image, canvas or video OCR An icon with no text or id Image matching A device with no UI tree, watched through a camera OCR and image matching. See Production devices The same word appears in several places OCR with an area of interest or index Speed things up # Keep the UI tree first. List page source and element sources before screenshot sources, so vision only runs when it's needed. Search part of the screen. An area of interest crops the scree

d: Limit where Optics looks for an element, so repeated text can't be matched in the wrong place and vision runs faster.
x: An area of interest (AOI) is a rectangle on the screen. Give one to a step and Optics only accepts an element inside it. Use it when the same text appears in several places, such as an Add to cart button that also appears in a product description, or to make OCR faster by reading less of the screen. Set an area # Four values describe the rectangle, each as a percentage of the screen, from 0 to 100: Parameter Meaning Default aoi_x Left edge, from the left of the screen 0 aoi_y Top edge, from the top of the screen 0 aoi_width Width of the area 100 aoi_height Height of the area 100 The defaults cover the whole screen, which means "no area". Pass the values by name: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Add To Cart , Press Element , Add to cart , aoi_y=75 , aoi_height=25 This looks for Add to cart only in the bottom quarter: it starts 75% of the way down and covers the remaining 25%. Some common areas: Area Values Top half aoi_height=50 Bottom half aoi_y=50,aoi_height=50 Right third aoi_x=67,aoi_width=33 Centre aoi_x=25,aoi_y=25,aoi_width=50,aoi_height=50 The edges must stay on the screen: aoi_x plus aoi_width , and aoi_y plus aoi_height , can be at most 100. How it works # OCR and image matching crop the screenshot to the area before they search. They read less, so they're faster too. The UI tree can't be cropped. Optics finds the element as usual, then keeps it only if its centre is inside the area. Each step that uses an area saves a screenshot with the rectangle drawn on it ( …_with_aoi.jpg in execution_output/ ), so you can check you chose the right part of the screen. Keywords that accept an area # Press Element , Enter Text , Enter Number , Clear Element Text , Get Text , Swipe From Element and Scroll From Element . Checks such as Assert Presence don't take an area. In the Python library, only press_element accepts area parameters. Area or index? # Both pick one match out of several. Use index when you know which match you want by order (the second Add to cart button). Use an area when you know where it is, which keeps working when items are added or reordered. You can combine them. See also # Find elements by text and image Define elements Action keywords

t: Recover failing steps with AI self-heal
h: Install the AI engine and set your key
d: Let an AI model look at the screen and finish a step when every way of finding its element has failed.
x: AI self-heal is a last line of defence. When a step can't find its element by any value or any method, Optics sends a screenshot to an AI model and asks it to complete the step. If the button now says Log in instead of Sign in , the model can spot that and press it, and the test carries on. It's off by default. When to use it # Self-heal keeps long runs going through small, expected UI changes, such as monitoring a production app on a schedule, or a nightly regression where you'd rather get a full report than stop at the first renamed button. It isn't a substitute for good elements. A healed step passes , so a real change in the app can go unnoticed unless you read the logs. Fix the element afterwards, as described in Find out what healed . Turn it on # 1 Install the AI engine and set your key # Self-heal uses Google's Gemini models, the same as plain-English mode : $ optics setup --install llm $ export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key" 2 Enable it in config.yaml # config.yaml "c-mod" >ai_self_heal "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >llm_models "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >gemini "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true 3 Enable a screenshot source # The model works from a screenshot, so elements_sources must include one, such as appium_screenshot or playwright_screenshot . Without it, self-heal does nothing. If the AI engine isn't installed or the key is missing, Optics logs a warning and runs without self-heal. It never fails a run because self-heal is unavailable. What it does # When a step that finds an element fails, Optics gives the model: the step that failed and the element it was looking for, a screenshot of the screen, and the UI tree if there is one, the steps that ran just before. The model can take up to five actions to finish the step, using only six keywords: Press Element, Enter Text, Scroll, Swipe By Percentage, Press Keycode and Press By Percentage. Each action goes through Optics' normal ways of finding elements. If the step is done within five actions, it passes. If not, it fails with the original error. Self-heal covers steps that find an element and act on it: Press Element, Enter Text, Enter Number, Clear Element Text, Get Text, Swipe From Element, Scroll From Element, and the keywords built on them (Detect And Press, Select Dropdown Option). Checks such as Assert Presence don't self-heal, so a missing element still fails a check. Find out what healed # With optics execute and optics live , a healed step shows as passed. To see what happened, turn on file logs: config.yaml "c-mod" >file_log "c-dim" >: true Then search execution_output/internal_logs.log for AI self-heal : AI self-heal: attempting recovery for 'press_element' on 'Sign in' AI self-heal step 1/5 for 'press_element': action=keyword keyword=press_element params=['Log in'] reason=The button now reads 'Log in' AI self-heal: recovered 'press_element' via keyword 'press_element' Update the element with what the model used, here by adding sign_in,Log in to elements.csv . Over the HTTP API and MCP , a healed step's result says so directly, with "healed": true and the steps that worked. Costs and limits # Each healed step makes up to six calls to the model, and each call takes a few seconds and costs API usage. Screenshots are sent to Google while self-heal runs. Don't enable it on screens with data you can't share with a third party. Gemini is the only supported provider. The model's instructions are tuned for phones. It works in browsers, but key presses use Android key codes. See also # How Optics finds elements Describe a test in plain English config.yaml reference

h: What happens when a step fails
d: Check a suite without a device, run it for real, and choose which test cases run.
x: Two commands cover almost every run. optics dry_run checks your files without touching a device. optics execute runs the suite on the device or browser in your config.yaml and writes the results to execution_output/ . Check the suite first # $ optics dry_run birch-tests A dry run reads every file and checks that: every test step names a module or keyword that exists, every keyword in every module exists, with a suggestion when you mistype one, every ${name} is defined in an elements file. It doesn't tap, type or open anything, so it's quick and safe to run before every commit. It still starts the engines in your config.yaml , so they must be installed and a driver must be enabled. Run it # $ optics execute birch-tests Before the run, Optics checks that the target is reachable: for Appium, that the server answers and (on Android) that a device is connected; for Selenium, that the server answers. If not, it stops with a message saying what to start. Playwright needs no check. Then it runs Suite Setup , each test case in order, and Suite Teardown , and prints a live tree: Test Suite ├── Suite Setup | 1.21s | PASS │ └── Launch Birch | 1.21s | PASS ├── Shopper can sign in | 1.38s | PASS │ └── Sign In | 1.38s | PASS └── Shopper can add trail runners | 4.02s | FAIL ├── Sign In | 1.31s | PASS └── Add To Cart | 2.71s | FAIL ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ Total Test Cases: 3 | Passed : 2 | Failed: 1 │ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ What happens when a step fails # The rest of that test case is skipped, and its unrun steps show as NOT_RUN . The next test case runs as normal. One broken flow doesn't hide problems elsewhere. A Failure details box after the tree names each failed step and why it failed. Exit codes # Code Meaning 0 Every test case passed. 1 At least one test case failed, or the run couldn't start (no driver enabled, server unreachable, missing files). CI systems use this to mark a build as passed or failed. Choose which test cases run # List test cases to run, or to skip, in config.yaml . Names match exactly, ignoring case: config.yaml "c-mod" >include "c-dim" >: - Shopper can sign in Use include or exclude , not both. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown always run. There's no command-line option for this, so a common pattern in CI is a small config per job. See Organise a suite . Options # Option What it does --no-use-printer Print plain log output instead of the live tree. Useful when a CI log viewer garbles the tree. --runner pytest Run the suite through pytest instead of Optics' own runner. Most projects don't need this. To skip the reachability check, for example when the server is behind a proxy the check can't see, set OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 . How long steps wait # Action keywords act on the screen as it is. They don't wait for it to change. Checks wait: Keyword Waits up to Assert Presence , Assert Visibility 30 seconds Validate Element 10 seconds Detect And Press 30 seconds, then carries on without failing Pass a different time as the second value: Assert Presence,Welcome,60 . Put a check after any step that loads a new screen, so the next action doesn't run too early. See also # Read the results Run tests in CI CLI reference

d: Find out what happened in a run from the JUnit report, the screenshots and the logs.
x: Every run writes its results to execution_output/ inside the project folder. The terminal tree tells you what failed. The files tell you why . What a run writes # birch-tests/execution_output/ ├── junit_output.xml # pass/fail for every test, for CI ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-pre_press_element.jpg # the screen before each step ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-11-…-press_element_element_detection_result.jpg ├── 2026-10-09T14-02-15-…-end_of_run.jpg # the last screen ├── page_sources_log.xml # the UI tree, captured during the run ├── internal_logs.log # with file_log: true ├── execution_logs.log # with file_log: true └── logs.json # with json_log: true File When it's written Use it to junit_output.xml Every run Show results in CI. Standard JUnit XML that GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins and others read. …pre_<keyword>.jpg Before each step that finds an element See what was on screen when the step started. …_detection_result.jpg When Optics found an element by position See exactly what Optics found, boxed in green. …_with_aoi.jpg When a step uses an area of interest Check the area covers the right part of the screen. It's drawn in blue. …end_of_run.jpg At the end of the run See where the app was left. page_sources_log.xml or .html When the UI tree is read Find the right XPath or text for an element. internal_logs.log , execution_logs.log With file_log: true Read every attempt Optics made, including which ways of finding an element failed. logs.json With json_log: true Feed results into your own dashboards. detected_errors_<id>.json When an error screen was found See which error definition matched. Investigate a failure # Read the Failure details box in the terminal. It names the test case, the step and the reason. **Open the last pre_… screenshot** before the failure. Is the screen what you expected? If it shows a loading spinner, the step ran too early: add an Assert Presence before it. If it shows a different screen, an earlier step went somewhere unexpected. Search the logs for the element's value. With file_log: true , execution_logs.log has a line for every attempt, such as Trying … on 'Sign in' ... FAIL . **Reproduce it in optics live .** Run the steps before the failure, then try the failing step with different values until one works. See Record a test . Turn on more logging # Add these to config.yaml : config.yaml "c-mod" >file_log "c-dim" >: true # write internal_logs.log and execution_logs.log "c-mod" >json_log "c-dim" >: true # write logs.json, a list of every run event "c-mod" >log_level "c-dim" >: DEBUG # more detail in the terminal and log files log_level takes DEBUG , INFO (the default), WARNING or ERROR . Use WARNING to keep the terminal quiet so the tree stands out. Read the JUnit report # junit_output.xml has one <testcase> per test case, with a <failure> when it failed. Inside each, Optics records every module and keyword with its status and timing, so CI tools that show nested steps display the same tree you saw in the terminal. If error screens were detected, the report has an extra failing test case called on-screen-error-detection . See Catch error screens . Keep the folder tidy # Screenshots from every run accumulate in execution_output/ . Clear the folder before runs where you need clean results, such as in CI: $ rm -rf birch-tests/execution_output $ optics execute birch-tests To write results somewhere else, set execution_output_path in config.yaml . A relative path is relative to the folder you run optics from, and the folder must exist. See also # Catch error screens Run tests in CI Troubleshooting

h: What happens at the end of a run
d: Fail a run in CI when the app ends on a crash dialog, a "Session expired" message or any other error you define.
x: Some failures don't break a step. The app shows Session expired , or Android shows Birch has stopped , and the test still passes because no step looked for that message. Error detection catches these. You list the messages that mean something went wrong, and Optics checks the screen for them at the end of every run. 1 List the error messages # Create a CSV anywhere in the project. The template uses test_data/error_definitions.csv : test_data/error_definitions.csv error_code,match_string,description,severity ERR_CRASH , has stopped , The app crashed with a system dialog , critical ERR_NOT_RESPONDING , isn't responding , Android shows an ANR dialog , critical ERR_SESSION , Session expired , The user was signed out , high ERR_NETWORK , No internet connection , The app lost its connection , medium ERR_SERVER , Something went wrong , The server returned an error page , high Column Required What it's for error_code Yes A short name for the error. It appears in the report. match_string Yes Text that means this error is on screen. description No What the error means, for whoever reads the report. severity No Any label you like, such as critical or low . 2 Run the suite as usual # $ optics execute birch-tests There's nothing to switch on. If the project has an error definitions file, Optics uses it. What happens at the end of a run # After the last test case, Optics captures the screen one more time, reads all the text in the app's UI tree, and looks for each match_string . Matching ignores case and finds the text anywhere: session expired matches Your session expired. Please sign in again. For each match, Optics: logs a warning, which you can read in execution_logs.log when file_log: true is set: ON-SCREEN ERROR DETECTED — code: ERR_SESSION | matched_on: match_string | match_string: 'Session expired' | severity: high | The user was signed out , adds a failing test case named on-screen-error-detection to junit_output.xml , with one failure per match, writes the details to execution_output/detected_errors_<id>.json . CI tools that read the JUnit report then show the run as failed, even though every step passed. On Optics 1.10.5, an all-pass run can leave the entry out When every test case passes, Optics 1.10.5 can finish the JUnit report before the error-detection entry is added, so the report shows no failure. The match is still written to detected_errors_<id>.json , and to execution_logs.log with file_log: true . Until a release fixes this, have CI check detected_errors_<id>.json as well as the JUnit report. The exit code doesn't change A detected error appears in the JUnit report but doesn't change the exit code of optics execute . If your CI decides pass or fail from the exit code alone, have it read the JUnit report as well. See Run tests in CI . Write good match strings # Use a phrase only an error would show. has stopped is good. Error matches too much, such as a help page about error messages. Copy the exact words from a screenshot of the error, and keep them short. Matching is plain text, not a pattern, so * or .* are matched literally. Avoid text that appears in your own tests. A match anywhere on the last screen counts. Limits # The check runs once, on the last screen. If the app recovers before the run ends, the error isn't seen. Add an explicit check in your test for errors that can appear and disappear mid-flow, such as Assert Presence on the screen you expect next. It needs the app's UI tree. On production devices driven through a camera, there's no tree to read. It's skipped if the session is already closed, for example when Suite Teardown ran Close And Terminate App . To keep the check, don't close the app in Suite Teardown. Definitions are CSV only. optics dry_run , optics live , the HTTP API and MCP don't run the check. See also # Read the results Run tests in CI Project files reference

d: Run the same suite on every pull request and read the results in your CI system.
x: A suite earns its keep when it runs on every change. In CI, Optics needs the same three things as on your machine: Optics itself, the engines in your config.yaml , and something to drive. d: Use this checklist before you rely on a suite in CI or for production monitoring.
x: A suite that passes on your laptop can still be flaky, slow or hard to debug in CI. Work through these items before the team starts trusting its results. Your ticks are saved in this browser, so you can come back to the list. The suite # Every test case has a clear outcome in its name. Shopper can add a backpack tells whoever reads a failure what broke. Test 3 doesn't. Every screen change is followed by a check. Action keywords don't wait. Put Assert Presence or Validate Element after any step that loads a new screen, instead of Sleep . See Run a suite . Important elements have a fallback. Give key buttons and fields a second value, usually their visible text, so one renamed id doesn't fail the run. See Define elements . No test relies on another. Each test case should be able to run on its own, with Suite Setup handling shared setup. Check with include: in config.yaml . ** optics dry_run passes.** Run it before every commit, and as the first CI step. The configuration # The Optics version is pinned in CI ( optics-framework==1.10.5 ). Upgrade on purpose, in its own change. Only the engines you use are enabled. Detected error screens only show up in the JUnit report. See Run tests in CI . Screenshots are kept when a run fails. Upload execution_output/ as a CI artifact. A suite people learn to ignore is worse than no suite. If you use AI features # Healed steps are reviewed. With AI self-heal on, a healed step passes.
