h: Install the Appium server and its Android driver
Start an emulator or connect a phone
Find the app's package and activity
d: Set up Appium and adb, then run your tests on an Android phone or emulator.
x: Optics drives Android apps through Appium , an open-source server that taps, types and reads the screen on a device. You run the Appium server on your machine, Optics talks to it, and Appium talks to the phone or emulator over adb (Android Debug Bridge, the SDK's device tool). This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the package name com.birch.shop . Replace it with your own app. Before you begin # You need: Optics installed. See Install Optics . Node.js 20 or newer, to run the Appium server. The Android SDK. We recommend getting it with Android Studio , which also creates emulators. An emulator, or an Android phone and a USB cable. Set up # 1 Install the Appium engine # $ optics setup --install appium This adds the Python client that Optics uses to talk to Appium. It doesn't install the server. 2 Install the Appium server and its Android driver # $ npm install -g appium $ appium driver install uiautomator2 UiAutomator2 is the Appium driver for Android. It needs the ANDROID_HOME environment variable set to your SDK folder, and Java installed. Run appium driver doctor uiautomator2 to check both. 3 Make adb available # adb ships in the SDK's platform-tools folder. Add that folder to your PATH, then check it: $ adb version On macOS the SDK is usually in ~/Library/Android/sdk , on Linux in ~/Android/Sdk , and on Windows in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk . 4 Start an emulator or connect a phone # For an emulator, open Android Studio's Device Manager and start a virtual device. For a phone, turn on Developer options (tap Build number seven times in Settings > About phone ), then turn on USB debugging . Connect the cable and accept the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt on the phone. Check that adb sees it: $ adb devices List of devices attached emulator-5554 device The first column is the device's serial. device in the second column means it's ready. unauthorized means you still need to accept the prompt on the phone. 5 Find the app's package and activity # Optics needs the app's package (its id, such as com.birch.shop ) and its activity (the screen it opens on). Open the app on the device, then ask adb what has focus: $ adb shell dumpsys window | grep -E 'mCurrentFocus' mCurrentFocus=Window{4f2a1c u0 com.birch.shop/com.birch.shop.MainActivity} The part before the / is the package, and the part after it is the activity. If you know the package, you can also ask Android for its launch activity: $ adb shell cmd package resolve-activity --brief com.birch.shop priority=0 preferredOrder=0 match=0x108000 specificIndex=-1 isDefault=true com.birch.shop/.MainActivity An activity that starts with a dot is short for the package plus that name: .MainActivity means com.birch.shop.MainActivity . 6 Write config.yaml # Create a project with optics init birch-android , then replace its config.yaml : config.yaml "c-mod" >driver_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >appium "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >url "c-dim" >: "http://127.0.0.1:4723" # where the Appium server listens "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: # must not be empty "c-mod" >platformName "c-dim" >: Android # required; picks the Android setup "c-mod" >automationName "c-dim" >: UiAutomator2 "c-mod" >deviceName "c-dim" >: emulator-5554 "c-mod" >udid "c-dim" >: emulator-5554 # optional; pins one device "c-mod" >appPackage "c-dim" >: com.birch.shop # app opened by "Launch App" with no value "c-mod" >appActivity "c-dim" >: com.birch.shop.MainActivity # appium:settings: {allowInvisibleElements: true} # optional; include off-screen elements "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >appium_find_element "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} # asks Appium for XPaths, ids and text - "c-mod" >appium_page_source "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} # searches the app's UI tree - "c-mod" >appium_screenshot "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} # screenshots for OCR and image matching "c-mod" >text_detection "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >easyocr "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} # needs: optics setup --install easyocr "c-mod" >imag

h: Install the Appium server and the XCUITest driver
Install the app and find its bundle id
d: Set up Appium with the XCUITest driver, then run your tests on an iOS simulator or device.
x: Optics drives iOS apps through Appium and its XCUITest driver, which uses Apple's own UI testing tools. You run the Appium server on a Mac, and Optics talks to it. iOS testing needs macOS, because Xcode only runs there. This page uses Birch, a sample shoe store app with the bundle id com.birch.shop . Replace it with your own app. Before you begin # You need: A Mac with Xcode installed from the App Store. Open it once to accept the license and install its components, then run xcode-select --install for the command-line tools. Optics installed. See Install Optics . Node.js 20 or newer, to run the Appium server. A build of your app: a .app for the simulator, or a signed build for a real device. Set up # 1 Install the Appium engine # $ optics setup --install appium 2 Install the Appium server and the XCUITest driver # $ npm install -g appium $ appium driver install xcuitest 3 Start a simulator # List the simulators Xcode provides: $ xcrun simctl list devices == Devices == -- iOS 17.5 -- iPhone 15 (5D1C2A60-8F0E-4B7A-9C41-2E6F0C3B9A17) (Shutdown) iPhone 15 Pro (A3E9F7B2-1C44-4D2B-8E0A-7B5D9C6E2F01) (Shutdown) Boot one by name and open the Simulator app to watch it: $ xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 15" $ open -a Simulator 4 Install the app and find its bundle id # Install your simulator build, then read its bundle id , the app's unique name: $ xcrun simctl install booted Birch.app $ plutil -extract CFBundleIdentifier raw Birch.app/Info.plist com.birch.shop 5 Write config.yaml # Create a project with optics init birch-ios , then replace its config.yaml : config.yaml "c-mod" >driver_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >appium "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >url "c-dim" >: "http://127.0.0.1:4723" "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >platformName "c-dim" >: iOS # picks the iOS setup "c-mod" >automationName "c-dim" >: XCUITest "c-mod" >deviceName "c-dim" >: "iPhone 15" # the simulator's name "c-mod" >bundleId "c-dim" >: com.birch.shop # required: the app Launch App opens # udid: <device udid> # real devices "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >appium_find_element "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} - "c-mod" >appium_page_source "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} - "c-mod" >appium_screenshot "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} If you have several iOS versions installed, add platformVersion: "17.5" so Appium picks the right simulator. 6 Check the setup # $ optics doctor birch-ios Without bundleId , the doctor shows a failure, because XCUITest has nothing to launch: Project ✅ config: driver appium enabled ✅ config: appium element source enabled: appium_find_element, appium_page_source, appium_screenshot ❌ config: appium settings bundleId missing in capabilities → Edit config.yaml in this project folder. The adb rows in the Mobile section are for Android. Ignore them on iOS, even when the doctor lists the adb hint under "Before your first real run". 7 Start Appium and run # Start the server in a second terminal and leave it running: $ appium Then run the tests: $ optics execute birch-ios Before the run, Optics checks that the Appium server answers at url . Set OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 to skip that check. The first session on a new simulator takes a few minutes, because Appium builds its helper app, WebDriverAgent, and installs it. Test on a real device # A real iPhone or iPad needs a few more steps: Connect the device, trust the Mac, and turn on Developer Mode in Settings > Privacy & Security . Find its id with xcrun xctrace list devices and set it as udid under capabilities . Sign WebDriverAgent with your Apple developer team, so it can be installed on the device. Signing is the step that most often goes wrong. Follow the Appium XCUITest driver docs for real-device setup. Write steps for iOS # iOS elements have types such as XCUIElementTypeButton and attributes such as name , label and value . Use them in XPaths: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID email_field , //XCUIElementTypeTextField[@name='Email'] password_field , //XCUIEleme

h: Run in CI without a screen
d: Set up Playwright or Selenium, then run your tests in a browser.
x: Optics tests websites with one of two drivers. Playwright starts a browser on your machine and needs no server. Selenium sends commands to a WebDriver server, such as a Selenium Grid, which runs the browser. We recommend Playwright unless you already run a Selenium Grid, or need Firefox or a real Chrome on remote machines. The examples use the Sauce Labs demo store , which you can sign in to with standard_user / secret_sauce . Set up # Install the engine. Optics also downloads the Chromium browser that Playwright uses: $ optics setup --install playwright Then enable the driver and its three element sources: config.yaml "c-mod" >driver_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >playwright "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true # no url and no server needed "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >browser "c-dim" >: chromium # ignored on 1.10.5: always Chromium "c-mod" >headless "c-dim" >: false # ignored on 1.10.5: always a visible window # viewport: {width: 1280, height: 800} # ignored on 1.10.5: always 1280×800 "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >playwright_find_element "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} - "c-mod" >playwright_page_source "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} - "c-mod" >playwright_screenshot "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} Note On Optics 1.10.5, Playwright ignores browser , headless and viewport under capabilities . It always opens a visible Chromium window at 1280×800. You can leave the keys in place for when they take effect. There's no server to start, so optics execute skips its preflight check for Playwright. Enter Text and Get Text fail in browsers on Optics 1.10.5 On 1.10.5, Enter Text and Get Text fail in Playwright with Object of type Locator is not JSON serializable . Both are fixed in the next release ( pull request #600 ). Until you upgrade, click the field, then type into it: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Sign in , Press Element , ${username_field} Sign in , Enter Text Direct , standard_user Install the engine: $ optics setup --install selenium Selenium needs a WebDriver server. The quickest is Selenium's Docker image, which runs Chrome inside a container: $ docker run -d -p 4444:4444 selenium/standalone-chrome For Firefox, use selenium/standalone-firefox . If you already run a Selenium Grid, point url at it instead. Then enable the driver and its element sources: config.yaml "c-mod" >driver_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >selenium "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >url "c-dim" >: "http://localhost:4444/wd/hub" # your Grid or standalone server "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: # must not be empty "c-mod" >browserName "c-dim" >: chrome # required: chrome or firefox "c-mod" >browserURL "c-dim" >: "https://www.saucedemo.com" # page opened when the browser starts "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >selenium_find_element "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} - "c-mod" >selenium_page_source "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} - "c-mod" >selenium_screenshot "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} capabilities must include browserName , and only chrome and firefox work. optics configure writes capabilities: {} for Selenium, which can't start, so add these keys by hand. Other keys under capabilities are passed to the browser as WebDriver capabilities. Before each run, optics execute checks that the server answers at url . If it doesn't, Optics stops with a "Cannot start" panel. Set OPTICS_SKIP_PREFLIGHT=1 to skip the check. Then check the setup and run your tests: $ optics doctor my-web-tests $ optics execute my-web-tests Open the site # Launch App starts the browser. How it picks the page depends on the driver: Step Playwright Selenium Launch App,https://www.saucedemo.com Opens the browser at that URL. Opens the browser at that URL the first time. Launch App with no URL Opens a blank page. Opens browserURL , or a blank page if it isn't set. Launch Other App,https://www.saucedemo.com/cart.html Opens the URL in a new tab. Goes to the URL in the current tab. We recommend putting the URL in the Launch Ap

d: Drive Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps with remote-control keys.
x: Optics tests TV apps through Appium , the same server it uses for phones. Each TV platform has its own Appium driver, and you pick it with platformName in config.yaml . On a TV you move around with remote-control keys and check what's on screen with assertions. TV platform platformName Appium driver How you move around Android TV Android UiAutomator2 Android key numbers, plus taps and typing Samsung Tizen TizenTV appium-tizen-tv-driver Remote key names only LG webOS LGTV appium-lg-webos-driver Remote key names only The examples use a TV app for Birch, a sample shoe store, with rows of shoes such as "Trail Runner 2" and "Pace Knit". Those steps belong to each Appium driver, and its project page covers them. Android TV # Android TV uses the same setup as an Android phone. h: Pair the dongle with the device
Point the camera at the screen
d: Test locked devices and live apps through a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard and a camera.
x: Optics can test a device with no automation software on it at all. A BLE dongle (a small USB Bluetooth adapter) pairs with the device as an ordinary Bluetooth mouse and keyboard. A camera pointed at the screen shows Optics what's there. Optics finds things in the camera picture with OCR and image matching, then moves the pointer and taps. When to use it # Use this setup when the usual drivers can't reach the device: USB debugging or developer mode isn't allowed , for example on locked company phones or retail devices. The app blocks screenshots , as banking and streaming apps often do. The camera sees the screen anyway. You monitor the live app. Synthetic monitoring runs the same journey on a real, unmodified device and app, the way a customer would. If you can use Appium or a browser driver, do. They're faster, read the UI tree directly, and support every keyword. What you need # A USB serial BLE HID dongle. It plugs into your machine as a serial port, and pairs with the device as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard. A way to see the screen. Either a camera or capture card that your machine sees as a webcam, or a TCP frame server that sends a picture on request. An OCR engine , such as EasyOCR, to read text in the camera picture. Image templates (optional), cropped pictures of icons that have no text. See Find elements by text and image . A stand that holds the camera square over the screen, so the picture doesn't shift between runs. Set up # 1 Install the engines # $ optics setup --install ble easyocr The ble engine adds serial-port support. The camera source and image matching need no extra install. 2 Pair the dongle with the device # Plug the dongle into your machine. On the device, open Bluetooth settings and pair with the dongle like any keyboard. A pointer appears on screen once it's connected. 3 Find the dongle's serial port # System Command Looks like macOS ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 Linux ls /dev/ttyACM* /dev/ttyACM0 Windows Device Manager, under Ports (COM & LPT) COM3 Instead of a path, you can give the dongle's USB product description, such as MZ-BLE-VMK-001-v1.2.1 . Optics finds the matching port for you, which helps when the port number changes between reboots. 4 Point the camera at the screen # Mount the camera straight on, with the screen upright and filling the picture edge to edge. Optics turns positions in the camera picture straight into pointer moves, so anything around the screen throws the taps off. 5 Write config.yaml # config.yaml "c-mod" >driver_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >ble "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >device_id "c-dim" >: "Birch test phone" # a label for the device "c-mod" >port "c-dim" >: /dev/ttyACM0 # or the dongle's USB product description "c-mod" >pixel_width "c-dim" >: 1080 # size of the screen in the camera picture "c-mod" >pixel_height "c-dim" >: 2336 "c-mod" >mickeys_width "c-dim" >: 1080 # pointer units to cross the screen "c-mod" >mickeys_height "c-dim" >: 2336 "c-mod" >x_invert "c-dim" >: 1 # -1 if the pointer moves the wrong way "c-mod" >y_invert "c-dim" >: 1 "c-mod" >elements_sources "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >camera_screenshot "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >enabled "c-dim" >: true "c-mod" >capabilities "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >camera_index "c-dim" >: 0 # or url: "192.168.1.20:9000" for a frame server "c-mod" >text_detection "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >easyocr "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} "c-mod" >image_detection "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >templatematch "c-dim" >: {enabled: true} 6 Calibrate, then run # Follow Calibrate the pointer below, then start the app on the device by hand and run: $ optics execute birch-production There's no preflight for this setup, so check the dongle and camera before you start a long run. Settings # ble driver # Name Default What it does device_id Required A name for the device. port Required The dongle's serial port ( /dev/ttyACM0 , /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 , COM3 ), or its USB product description. pixel_width , pixel_height

d: Add data, logic and integrations to your suites once the basics are in place.
x: Most suites never need the features in this section. A list of modules with good elements and a few checks covers most user flows. Reach for these when a flow depends on data, needs to branch, or when another system needs to drive Optics. Logic and data # Variables Store values, compute new ones, and use them in later steps. Data-driven tests Run one flow once per row of a data file. Conditions and loops Branch on what's on screen, and repeat modules. Call APIs in a test Fetch or create data over HTTP mid-test, and use the response in later steps. Integrate # Run keywords over HTTP Drive a device from your own service with optics serve . Generate pytest or Robot code Turn a suite into code you can extend. Let your AI agent build tests Connect optics mcp to Claude, Cursor or any MCP client. Use Optics from Python Call keywords from your own scripts. How logic runs in a suite Flow-control keywords run other modules. Steps inside those modules work slightly differently from top-level steps: they use only the first value of each element, and they don't accept name=value parameters. Keep modules that run inside loops and conditions simple, and give their elements a reliable first value.

h: Declare run-time variables for dry runs
d: Store values, compute new ones during a run, and use them in later steps.
x: In Optics, a variable is an element that holds a value instead of a locator. You define some in your elements file, and some keywords create or change them while the test runs. Any step can then use the value with ${name} . Define a variable # Add a row to an elements file, like any element: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID email , ava@birch.shop search_term , trail runner discount_code , WELCOME10 modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Search , Enter Text , ${search_bar} , ${search_term} Where ${name} works # As a whole value. ${search_term} on its own in a cell is replaced by the variable's value. When a variable has several values, they're tried in order, the same as element fallbacks . Not inside other text. Hello ${name} and @:${password} are used exactly as written; Optics doesn't replace part of a value. Store the whole value in a variable instead. Inside expressions. A few keywords read ${name} anywhere in their text: the expressions in Evaluate and Condition , the query in Read Data , and the URL, headers and body of an API call in Invoke API . These use the variable's first value. Create variables during a run # These keywords write a variable. Write the name of the variable on its own, without ${} : Keyword Writes Example Evaluate The result of an expression Evaluate,total,${price} + 5 Date Evaluate A date some days away Date Evaluate,delivery_date,${order_date},+5 days Read Data A value from a CSV or JSON file, or an environment variable Read Data,admin_email,test_data/users.csv,role == 'admin';select=email Invoke API Values from an API response See Call APIs in a test Run Loop The current item, once per pass See Data-driven tests modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Check Total , Evaluate , expected_total , ${price} * 2 Check Total , Assert Presence , ${expected_total} Writing ${total} as the name Evaluate,${total},${price} + 5 doesn't create total . Optics replaces ${total} before the keyword runs, so the step fails with "Element not found: total", or writes to a variable named after its old value. Write Evaluate,total,${price} + 5 . Declare run-time variables for dry runs # optics dry_run checks that every ${name} is defined, but it doesn't run the keywords that create variables. Add a placeholder row for each variable a keyword creates, so the dry run passes. The keyword replaces the placeholder during the real run: test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID price , 64 expected_total , placeholder This works for Evaluate , Read Data , Invoke API and Run Loop . Don't add a placeholder for Date Evaluate : in Optics 1.10.5 it adds its result after the placeholder instead of replacing it, so ${delivery_date} would give placeholder . The dry run reports the date variable as missing, which you can ignore. Values are text # Every value is text, even when it looks like a number. That matters in expressions: Evaluate puts the value into the expression as you wrote it. ${price} + 5 with price set to 64 becomes 64 + 5 , which is 69 . To join text, quote it: '${first_name}' + ' ' + '${last_name}' . Condition puts quotes around each value. ${count} == '3' works. ${count} > 2 fails, because it compares text with a number. Compare against quoted text, or compute the comparison with Evaluate first. See Conditions and loops . Evaluate allows arithmetic ( + - * / % ** ), comparisons, and , or , not and x if condition else y . It doesn't allow function calls such as int() . Hide sensitive values # Start a value with @: to keep it out of log files: password,@:correct-horse . Optics logs **** and types the value without the prefix, on Appium, Selenium and Bluetooth devices. Playwright types the prefix too. For real secrets, don't commit them at all. Read them from the environment at run time: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Sign In , Read Data , password , ENV:BIRCH_PASSWORD Sign In , Enter Text , ${password_field} , ${password} Add pa

h: Tap something only if it appears
Rules for modules run by these keywords
d: Run different modules depending on what's on screen or in a variable, and handle optional screens such as popups.
x: Most tests follow one path. Sometimes the app doesn't: a welcome popup appears only on first launch, a returning user skips sign-in, or a feature is behind a flag. Optics handles these with three keywords: Detect And Press for optional taps, Condition for branches, and Execute Module for running one module from another. Tap something only if it appears # For a popup that may or may not show, Detect And Press waits for the element and taps it if it appears. If it doesn't, the step still passes: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Launch Birch , Launch App Launch Birch , Detect And Press , Allow notifications , 5 Launch Birch , Detect And Press , Not now , 5 The second value is how many seconds to wait (30 by default). Keep it short: the step always waits the full time when the element never appears. Branch with Condition # Condition checks one or more conditions in order and runs the module paired with the first one that's true: Condition, <condition 1>, <module 1>, <condition 2>, <module 2>, …, <otherwise module> The last module, with no condition in front of it, runs when nothing matched. It's optional. Branch on what's on screen # A condition can be a module name . Optics runs that module: if it passes, the condition is true. Write a small module that checks for something, and use it as the test: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Is Signed In , Assert Presence , Picked for you , 5 Start Shopping , Condition , Is Signed In , Go To Search , Sign In If the home screen's Picked for you appears within 5 seconds, Optics runs Go To Search . Otherwise it runs Sign In . Put ! in front to flip a condition: Condition,!Is Signed In,Sign In . Warning The checking module really runs, so keep it to checks with short timeouts. A failed check waits its full timeout, and an action in it would change the app. Branch on a variable # A condition can also be an expression that compares variables: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3,param_4,param_5 Choose Flow , Condition , ${account_type} == 'business' , Business Checkout , ${account_type} == 'gift' , Gift Checkout , Standard Checkout Optics puts each variable's value in quotes before checking, so always compare with quoted text : ${account_type} == 'business' , ${count} == '3' . Compare numbers # Because values are compared as text, ${count} > 5 fails. Compute the comparison with Evaluate first, then check its result: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2,param_3 Check Cart , Evaluate , cart_is_big , ${count} > 5 Check Cart , Condition , ${cart_is_big} == 'True' , Offer Free Shipping Evaluate puts values into the expression without quotes, so ${count} > 5 works there and stores True or False . Declare cart_is_big,placeholder in your elements file for dry runs. Run one module from another # Execute Module runs a module's steps as part of another module: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Buy Trail Runners , Execute Module , Sign In Buy Trail Runners , Execute Module , Search For Shoes Buy Trail Runners , Press Element , Add to cart A module name written on its own as a step doesn't run that module. Use Execute Module . Rules for modules run by these keywords # Modules run by Condition , Execute Module and Run Loop follow simpler rules than top-level steps: Each element uses only its first value . Fallbacks don't apply. ** name=value parameters aren't available.** Give values in order: Assert Presence,Picked for you,5 , not timeout_str=5 . Their steps don't appear separately in the run tree. A failure message names the step that failed. If a branch needs fallbacks, give it its own test case instead and choose which test cases run with include and exclude in config.yaml . See also # Variables Data-driven tests Flow control keywords

d: Call an HTTP API in the middle of a test, check the response, and use values from it in later steps.
x: Some steps are faster or more reliable through an API than through the screen: creating a test account, fetching today's offer code, or checking that an order reached the backend. Invoke API calls an endpoint you describe in a YAML file, checks the response, and saves values from it as variables for later steps. The example on this page runs as written. It uses DummyJSON , a free public API for testing. 1 Describe the API # Create a YAML file anywhere in the project, with a top-level api: key. Group endpoints into collections , each with a base URL: test_data/api.yaml "c-mod" >api "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >collections "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >dummyjson "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >name "c-dim" >: "DummyJSON" "c-mod" >base_url "c-dim" >: "https://dummyjson.com" "c-mod" >global_headers "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >content-type "c-dim" >: "application/json" "c-mod" >apis "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >login "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >name "c-dim" >: "Sign in" "c-mod" >endpoint "c-dim" >: "/auth/login" "c-mod" >request "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >method "c-dim" >: POST "c-mod" >body "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >username "c-dim" >: " ${api_username} " "c-mod" >password "c-dim" >: " ${api_password} " "c-mod" >expected_result "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >jsonpath_assertions "c-dim" >: - "c-mod" >path "c-dim" >: $.accessToken "c-mod" >condition "c-dim" >: "len($) > 0" "c-mod" >extract "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >access_token "c-dim" >: $.accessToken "c-mod" >me "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >name "c-dim" >: "Who am I" "c-mod" >endpoint "c-dim" >: "/auth/me" "c-mod" >request "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >method "c-dim" >: GET "c-mod" >headers "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >Authorization "c-dim" >: "Bearer ${access_token} " "c-mod" >expected_result "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >extract "c-dim" >: "c-mod" >email "c-dim" >: $.email ** request ** sets the method, headers and a JSON body. ${name} is replaced anywhere in the endpoint, headers and body. ** jsonpath_assertions ** checks the response. path picks a value, and condition is a small expression where $ stands for that value. A false condition fails the step. ** extract ** saves values from the response as variables, using JSONPath: $.accessToken , $.customer.id , $.items[0].name . 2 Add the inputs to your elements file # test_data/elements.csv Element_Name,Element_ID api_username , emilys api_password , emilyspass access_token , placeholder email , placeholder The placeholder rows let optics dry_run accept variables that only get their value during the run. 3 Call the endpoints in a module # Refer to an endpoint as collection.name : modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1 Sign In Over The API , Invoke API , dummyjson.login Sign In Over The API , Invoke API , dummyjson.me Add a test case that runs the module: test_cases/test_cases.csv test_case,test_step API sign in works , Sign In Over The API The first call signs in and saves access_token . The second sends the token and saves the account's email . From here, any step can use ${email} : type it into a field, check it on screen, or compare it in a condition . A project with only API steps still needs a config.yaml with a driver enabled, but the driver doesn't open anything unless a step asks it to. 4 Run it # $ optics execute api-demo └── API sign in works | 1.31s | PASS └── Sign In Over The API | 1.31s | PASS ├── Invoke API (dummyjson.login) | 0.66s | PASS └── Invoke API (dummyjson.me) | 0.64s | PASS Every request and response is logged to execution_output/api_details.log , and to api_details.har , which you can open in a browser's developer tools. Combine API and UI steps # A common pattern is to set up data through the API, then check it in the app: modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Order Shows In App , Invoke API , birch.create_order Order Shows In App , Press Element , Orders Order Shows In App , Assert Presence , ${order_number} Creating the order through the API takes a second. d: Start a local Optics server and drive a device or browser from your own service, one keyword per request.
x: optics serve runs Optics as a small web server on your machine. Another program, such as an internal dashboard, a test orchestrator or a script in another language, can then open a session on a device and run keywords on it with plain HTTP requests. Each request runs one keyword and returns its result. Use the server when something other than Optics decides what to do next. If you want to run a suite, optics execute is simpler. If an AI agent is the caller, use MCP instead. 1 Start the server # $ optics serve It listens on http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Check it's up: $ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health {"status":"Optics Framework API is running","version":"1.10.5"} Use --port to change the port. Interactive API docs are at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs while the server runs. 2 Start a session # A session is one connection to a device or browser. Send the same settings you'd put in config.yaml : $ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/start \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "driver_sources": ["playwright"], "elements_sources": ["playwright_find_element", "playwright_page_source", "playwright_screenshot"] }' {"session_id":"23db1bdc-07d8-4cca-bfaa-1e9deaf4b794","driver_id":"PLAYWRIGHT_SESSION","status":"created"} Keep the session_id . Starting a session also opens the app, as Launch App would. For a phone, pass an Appium entry with its URL and capabilities: { "driver_sources" : [{ "appium" : { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1: 4723 " , "capabilities" : { "platformName" : "Android" , "automationName" : "UiAutomator2" , "deviceName" : "emulator-5554" , "appPackage" : "com.birch.shop" , "appActivity" : ".MainActivity" }}}], "elements_sources" : [ "appium_find_element" , "appium_page_source" , "appium_screenshot" ] } 3 Run keywords # Send one keyword per request, with its values in order: $ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Launch Other App", "params": ["https://www.saucedemo.com"]}' {"execution_id":"ebbdc919-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":null}} $ curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/action \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"mode": "keyword", "keyword": "Assert Presence", "params": ["Accepted usernames are"]}' {"execution_id":"71f5ee34-…","status":"SUCCESS","data":{"result":true}} Keyword names work in any case: Assert Presence or assert_presence . params can also be an object of named values, such as {"element": "Login", "index": "1"} . A list inside it gives fallbacks: {"element": ["//input[@id='login-button']", "Login"]} . 4 Look at the screen # $ curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/screenshot \ | python3 -c 'import sys,json,base64; open("screen.png","wb").write(base64.b64decode(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["result"]))' /elements lists the elements on screen, and /source returns the UI tree. 5 Stop the session # $ curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/stop {"status":"terminated"} This closes the app and ends the session. Follow a session live # Two endpoints stream updates as server-sent events : /v1/sessions/{id}/events sends a message when each keyword starts, passes or fails. /v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/stream sends a new screenshot and element list whenever the screen changes, which is handy for showing a live view of the device. $ curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/$SESSION/events Keep the server safe # The server has no authentication , and it accepts requests from any web page your browser opens. Anyone who can reach it can control the connected device. Keep the default --host 127.0.0.1 , so only your machine can reach it. If another machine must call it, put it behind a proxy that adds authentication, on a trusted network. Run one worker (the default). Sessions live in the server's memory, so several workers would lose track of each other's sessions. See also # HTTP API reference , with every endpoint and field The OpenAPI document , for

d: Turn a CSV or YAML suite into a pytest or Robot Framework file you can extend with code.
x: optics generate reads a suite and writes the same test as code: a pytest file or a Robot Framework file. Use it when a suite needs logic the files can't express, or when you're moving a suite into a codebase that already runs everything through pytest or Robot. The generated file is a starting point. Once you edit it, it no longer follows the suite files, so keep the suite as the source of truth for as long as you can. Generate a file # $ optics generate birch-tests Generated test file: birch-tests/generated/Tests/test_generated.py Generated requirements file: birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt For Robot Framework: $ optics generate birch-tests --framework robot --output checkout.robot Option Default What it does --framework pytest pytest or robot . --output test_generated.py or test_generated.robot The file name. It's always written to <project>/generated/Tests/ . The project needs a file named exactly config.yaml , plus test cases, modules and an elements file. What you get # Each module becomes a function (or Robot keyword), each test case becomes a test, and elements become a dictionary: generated/Tests/test_generated.py ELEMENTS = { 'username_field' : "//input[@id='user-name']" , 'login_button' : "//input[@id='login-button']" , } def sign_in(optics: Optics) -> None : optics.enter_text(ELEMENTS[ 'username_field' ], 'standard_user' ) optics.press_element(ELEMENTS[ 'login_button' ]) optics.assert_presence( 'Products' ) def test_shopper_can_add_a_backpack(optics): open_the_store(optics) sign_in(optics) Run it with pytest from the generated/Tests folder: $ pip install -r birch-tests/generated/requirements.txt $ cd birch-tests/generated/Tests $ pytest test_generated.py Generated code fails to run on Optics 1.10.5 In 1.10.5, the generated file uses config names that Optics.setup() doesn't accept, and values containing single quotes break the Python syntax. A fix is on its way in the next release. Until then, in the generated file, rename driver_config to driver_sources , element_source_config to elements_sources , text_config to text_detection and image_config to image_detection , and write XPaths in your elements file with double quotes, such as //input[@id="user-name"] . What isn't converted # Only the first value of each element is used. Fallbacks are dropped. Pass a list to keep them: optics.press_element([ELEMENTS['login_button'], 'Login']) . Flow-control keywords (Run Loop, Condition, Read Data, Evaluate, Invoke API and others) and a few more, such as Select Dropdown Option, aren't converted. Steps that use them are left out of the generated code silently. Check the output against your modules. Suite Setup and Suite Teardown become ordinary tests. Image templates are copied only if they're in an input_templates/ folder at the project's top level. See also # Use Optics from Python Use Optics in Robot Framework CLI reference

h: Keywords that never fail a step
d: Every keyword you can use in a step, grouped by what it does.
x: A keyword is one action or check, such as Press Element or Assert Presence . Each row of a module is one keyword followed by its parameters. This page covers the rules every keyword shares, then lists all of them. modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Sign In , Enter Text , ${email_field} , ana@birch.example Sign In , Press Element , ${sign_in} Sign In , Assert Presence , Welcome , 20 Keyword names # Write keyword names in Title Case in CSV and YAML files: Press Element , Assert Presence . In optics live , the MCP server and Python, the same keyword is written in snake_case: press_element , assert_presence . The runner ignores capitalization and collapses spaces, so Press Element , press element and press_element all reach the same keyword. If you misspell a name, the error suggests the closest match. Run optics list to print every keyword name in snake_case. Parameters # Parameters are positional. They fill the keyword's parameters in the order shown in each parameter table on these pages. To set a parameter by name, write name=value . This works only when name is a real parameter of that keyword. Use it to skip parameters you want to leave at their defaults: Browse , Press Element , Trail Runner 2 , index=1 Here index=1 sets the fifth parameter of Press Element and leaves repeat , offset_x and offset_y at their defaults. Common mistake Leaving a cell empty doesn't skip a parameter. Empty cells are dropped, so the next value slides into the empty slot. Press By Percentage,50,90,,tap_cta sets repeat to tap_cta and fails. Write Press By Percentage,50,90,event_name=tap_cta instead. A value like text=Sign in or css=#cart stays positional, because text and css aren't parameter names. Values that start with / , // or ( are never treated as named, and == , != , <= and >= don't count as = . Note Steps inside a module that runs through Execute Module, Run Loop or Condition don't support name=value . Write every parameter positionally there. Every value is a string # Each keyword receives its parameters as text and converts them itself. Timeouts, counts, index , repeat , lengths and swipe percentages must be whole numbers. A decimal such as 2.5 fails the step. Timeouts are always in seconds. Element arguments # Many keywords take an element . Optics looks at the text you pass and decides what kind of locator it is. The checks run in this order, and the first match wins: If the value… Optics reads it as starts with text= Text to find on screen starts with text_only: Text to find with OCR (reading the screenshot) only, skipping the app's UI tree ends with .png , .jpg , .jpeg or .bmp An image file name to find on screen starts with css= A CSS selector starts with xpath= , / , // or ( An XPath, a path through the app's UI tree starts with android. or xcui A UI class name contains [ and ] , starts with . , or starts with # followed by a letter A CSS selector anything else Text to find on screen Text is matched against the app's UI tree first, then with OCR if you configured text detection. Image file names are matched by file name only, and Optics finds the file anywhere in your project folder. See Text and images for how matching works. Common mistake Plain text that looks like another locator type is read as that type. (optional) starts with ( , so it's read as an XPath. Price [USD] and .com are read as CSS selectors. Write text=(optional) , text=Price [USD] or text=.com to force text. Other pitfalls: id: locators always fail. No element source supports them. Use an XPath such as //*[@resource-id="com.birch.shop:id/cart"] . The text= prefix is understood by the Appium and Playwright element sources. OCR and Selenium search for the whole value, including text= , so use it only where you need it. The xpath= prefix works only on Playwright. Use a bare //… XPath on Appium and Selenium. .tif and .tiff files aren't treated as images. Save templates as .png . Most of the time you pass ${name} instead and define the locator

d: Learn how to start, switch, close and inspect the app or browser under test.
x: App management keywords start and stop the app or browser that your test drives. Most suites call Launch App in a setup module and Close And Terminate App in a teardown module. modules/modules.csv module_name,module_step,param_1,param_2 Open Birch , Launch App , com.birch.shop Close Birch , Close And Terminate App See Keywords for the rules all keywords share. Start and switch # Launch App # Starts the app or browser under test, or brings the app to the front. Parameter Default What it does app_identifier Empty Appium: the Android package or iOS bundle id. Playwright and Selenium: the URL to open. Empty uses the app from your config. app_activity Empty Appium on Android: the activity to start. Selenium: the browser name, chrome or firefox . event_name Empty Label for a timed event. See Event names . Open Birch , Launch App , com.birch.shop Open Birch , Launch App , com.birch.shop , com.birch.shop.MainActivity Open Birch Web , Launch App , https://birch.example - Launch App com.birch.shop Good to know: On Appium, Launch App starts a session if none is running. d: Every setting in a project's config.yaml.
x: A project's config.yaml tells Optics which driver to use, how to find elements, and where to write logs and results. Every setting lives in the project; there's no global config file and no environment variable that overrides it. Run optics configure to write a working file by answering a few questions, then edit it by hand with this page. How Optics finds the file # Command Which file it reads optics execute , optics dry_run Any YAML file in the project tree that has driver_sources and elements_sources . The file name doesn't matter. If there are several, the last one found wins. optics live The first YAML file in the project tree with any config key. optics doctor , optics configure , optics generate Exactly <folder>/config.yaml . optics serve , optics mcp None. Settings come from each session request. We recommend one file named config.yaml at the project root, so every command reads the same settings. Settings you leave out take their defaults. Optics ignores keys it doesn't know, so a typo such as log_levle is silently skipped. Warning If config.yaml has a wrong value type, optics execute logs the problem, skips the file and runs with defaults. The run then stops with "No driver enabled". Run optics doctor <folder> to find the problem. Top-level keys # Key Default What it does driver_sources All disabled The driver that controls the device or browser. See driver_sources . elements_sources All disabled Where Optics looks for elements: the driver's UI tree, its locators, or its screenshots. element_sources is accepted as an alias. text_detection All disabled OCR engines for finding elements by on-screen text. image_detection All disabled Engines for finding elements by image templates. llm_models All disabled The LLM for AI self-heal and the plain-English mode of optics live . log_level INFO DEBUG , INFO , WARNING , ERROR or CRITICAL , any case. Unknown values become INFO . file_log false Writes internal_logs.log and execution_logs.log to the output folder. log_path None One file for both logs instead of two. Used only with file_log: true . json_log false Writes a JSON array of every test, module and keyword event to logs.json at the end of the run. json_path None Where to write the JSON events instead of <output>/logs.json . ~ is expanded. console true Has no effect in 1.10.5. Nothing reads it. Use log_level to control console output. execution_output_path <project>/execution_output Where results, screenshots and logs go. Relative paths are relative to the folder you run optics from. include None Run only these test cases. See include and exclude . exclude None Skip these test cases. ai_self_heal false Lets an LLM try to recover when an element can't be found. See ai_self_heal . strict_element_match false Turns off fuzzy and partial text matching. See strict_element_match . save_captures true Whether Capture Screenshot , Capture Pagesource and Get Screen Elements write files. See save_captures . halt_duration 0.1 Seconds to wait after a keyword fails every fallback. It isn't a pause between steps. event_attributes_json None Path to a JSON file of event attributes. When it includes an eventUrl , events you label with event_name are sent there at the end of the session. project_path The project folder The CLI always sets this to the folder you pass, so leave it out. It only matters for the Python SDK. Note If you set execution_output_path yourself, create the folder first. JUnit results and logs create their own folders, but screenshots fail to save without a warning if the folder is missing. For a guided introduction, see Write a test and Write tests in YAML . How Optics finds your files # Optics walks the whole project folder, including subfolders, and decides what each .csv , .yml and .yaml file is by its content , not its name or location. You can use any folder layout. We recommend the one optics init creates: birch-tests/ ├── config.yaml ├── test_cases/test_cases.csv ├── modules/modules.csv ├── test_data/elements.csv └── test_data/error_definitions.csv # optional File type CSV: the header row must contain YAML: top-level key Test cases test_case and test_step Test Cases Modules module_name and module_step Modules Elements Element_Name and Element_ID Elements Error definitions error_code and match_string Not supported API definitions Not supported api Config Not applicable driver_sources and elements_sources A project needs at least one test cases file and one modules file. Elements, error definitions and API files are optional. You can split each type across several files. Common mistake Write column names and YAML keys exactly as shown. Optics recognizes element_name or test_cases: as the right file type, but then reads nothing from it, because the reader expects Element_Name and Test Cases . When two files define the same thing: Test cases and modules with the same name: the file read last wins, with a warning in the log. Elements with the same name: the values are combined into one fallback list. Image files ( .png , .jpg , .jpeg , .bmp ) anywhere in the project are available as image templates by file name. If two images share a name, one of them is used. Test cases # Each row adds one step to a test case. A step names a module. Rows with an empty name are skipped. test_step The name of a module to run. Rows with an empty step are skipped. Within a test case, the first failing step fails the test case and skips its remaining steps. The next test case still runs. Setup and teardown # Optics treats some test case names specially. Matching ignores case and looks for the words anywhere in the name. Name contains Role When it runs suite and setup Suite setup Once, before every other test case. If several match, the last one is used. suite and teardown Suite teardown Once, after every other test case. setup without suite Per-test setup Meant to run before each test. In 1.10.5 it runs only before the first test case. teardown without suite Per-test teardown Meant to run after each test. In 1.10.5 it runs only after the first test case. x: optics mcp runs a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a standard way for AI agents such as Claude, Cursor or VS Code to call outside tools. Your agent can start a session on a device or browser, look at the screen, and run Optics keywords one at a time. For a guided walkthrough, see Build tests with an AI agent . Install # The server needs the mcp extra. optics setup can't install it, and the all bundle doesn't include it. $ pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" You also need the extras for your driver, for example appium or playwright . See Engines and extras . Start the server # optics mcp [--transport stdio|http] [--host HOST] [--port PORT] Flag Default What it does --transport stdio stdio : your agent starts the server and talks to it directly. http : the server listens at http://<host>:<port>/mcp . --host 127.0.0.1 The address to listen on. http only. --port 8090 The port to listen on. http only. We recommend stdio for an agent on your own machine. Use http when the server runs in a container or on another machine. Connect your agent # Most agents read a JSON file that lists MCP servers. For Claude Desktop it's claude_desktop_config.json ; for Claude Code it's .mcp.json in your project. Other agents use the same shape. .mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "command" : "optics" , "args" : [ "mcp" ] } } } If your agent can't find optics , use the full path to it, for example /Users/ana/.optics/bin/optics . For the http transport, point the agent at the URL instead: .mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "optics" : { "url" : "http://127.0.0.1: 8090 /mcp" } } } When the server runs in Docker and Appium runs on your machine, pass url: "http://host.docker.internal:4723" to start_session . Session tools # start_session # Starts a session and launches the app. Returns {"session_id", "driver_id"} . Keep the session_id : every other tool needs it. Parameter Default What it does driver appium appium , selenium , playwright or ble . url Appium: http://127.0.0.1:4723 The driver's server URL. capabilities None The driver's capabilities, as in config.yaml . elements_sources The driver's three sources For example ["appium_find_element", "appium_page_source", "appium_screenshot"] . Passing [] makes the session fail to start. text_detection None OCR engines, for example ["easyocr"] . image_detection None Image engines, for example ["templatematch"] . project_path None A project folder. Optics loads its image templates. It doesn't load elements or test cases. ai_self_heal OPTICS_AI_SELF_HEAL , else off Turns on AI self-heal . llm_provider OPTICS_LLM_PROVIDER , else gemini The LLM provider for self-heal. llm_model OPTICS_LLM_MODEL , else gemini-2.5-flash The model for self-heal. strict_element_match Off Accepts only exact text matches. The first session against a remote device farm can take 30 to 60 seconds to start. terminate_session # Closes the app and ends the session. Takes session_id . Returns {"session_id", "status": "terminated"} . screenshot # Returns the current screen as a PNG image. Takes session_id . Keyword tools # Every app, action and verification keyword is a tool named after the keyword in snake_case. Each takes session_id plus the keyword's parameters. All parameter values are strings. Leave out a parameter to use its default. aoi_* stands for aoi_x , aoi_y , aoi_width and aoi_height , an area of the screen in percent (0–100). See Area of interest . Tool Parameters (defaults) launch_app app_identifier , app_activity , event_name launch_other_app app_name , event_name close_and_terminate_app none force_terminate_app app_name , event_name get_app_version app_package get_driver_session_id none start_appium_session event_name initialise_setup none Tool Parameters (defaults) press_element element , repeat (1), offset_x (0), offset_y (0), index (0), aoi_* , event_name detect_and_press element , timeout (30), event_name select_dropdown_option element , option , timeout (30), event_name enter_text element , text , aoi_* , event_name , in

d: Learn the endpoints `optics serve` exposes for starting sessions, running keywords and streaming results.
x: optics serve runs a local HTTP server that lets any language or tool drive a device through Optics. You start a session, send keywords one at a time, and read screenshots, UI trees and events back. For a guided introduction, see Drive Optics over HTTP . The machine-readable OpenAPI document is at https://optics-framework.org/openapi.json . Start the server # optics serve [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--workers N] Flag Default What it does --host 127.0.0.1 The address to listen on. --port 8000 The port to listen on. --workers 1 Server processes. Keep it at 1. Sessions live in each process's memory, so with more workers a request can reach a process that doesn't know your session and get a 404. The server prints its own log lines and Optics' debug logs to the terminal. Interactive docs are at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs while it runs. Warning The API has no authentication, and it accepts requests from any web origin (CORS is open). Anyone who can reach the port can control your devices. Keep the default 127.0.0.1 , and bind to another address only on a network you trust. The server doesn't read config.yaml or your project's test files. Each session gets its engines from the request. Sessions also don't write screenshots or page sources to disk, and they log at DEBUG . Endpoints # Method Path What it does GET / or /health Checks the server is up. Returns {"status": "Optics Framework API is running", "version": "1.10.5"} . POST /v1/sessions/start Starts a session from a SessionConfig and launches the app. Returns {"session_id", "driver_id", "status": "created"} . POST /v1/sessions/{id}/action Runs one keyword from an ExecuteRequest . Returns {"execution_id", "status": "SUCCESS", "data"} . POST /v1/sessions/{id}/templates Uploads an image template: {"name", "image_base64"} . The image can be raw base64 or a data: URL. Use the name as an element for the rest of the session. Returns {"name", "status": "ok"} . POST /v1/sessions/{id}/api Replaces the session's API definitions for Invoke API . Send {"api": {"collections": ...}} . Returns 204. GET /v1/sessions/{id}/screenshot The current screen. data.result is a base64 PNG without a data: prefix, or "" if the capture failed. GET /v1/sessions/{id}/driver-id The driver's own session id in data.result . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/variables Every variable in the session: {"variables": {"name": ["value", ...]}} . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/elements Elements on screen in data.result . Query: filter_config ( all , interactive , buttons , inputs , images , text ; repeatable) and compact=true . compact ignores the filter. Appium and Playwright only. GET /v1/sessions/{id}/source The UI tree or HTML. data is {"page_source", "timestamp"} directly, not under result . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/screen_elements A screenshot and its elements from the same frame. data is {"screenshot", "elements"} directly, not under result . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/events A stream of keyword events. See Streams . GET /v1/sessions/{id}/workspace/stream A stream of screenshots and elements whenever the screen changes. See Streams . GET /v1/keywords Every keyword, including flow control, with its description and parameters. DELETE /v1/sessions/{id}/stop Closes the app and ends the session. Returns {"status": "terminated"} . SessionConfig # The body of POST /v1/sessions/start . Every field is optional, but a session needs a driver and at least one element source. Field Type What it does driver_sources list The driver. Each item is a name ( "playwright" ) or {"appium": {"url": ..., "capabilities": {...}}} . A listed item is enabled unless it says "enabled": false . elements_sources list Element sources by name, for example ["appium_find_element", "appium_page_source", "appium_screenshot"] . There's no default here, so always list them. text_detection list OCR engines, for example ["easyocr"] . image_detection list Image engines, for example ["templatematch"] . project_path string A project folder on the server. Optics loads its image templates

d: Learn what each Optics error code means and how to fix it.
x: When a step or command fails, Optics usually attaches a code such as E0201 . The code tells you which part of Optics failed, and the message after it says why. This page lists every code in Optics 1.10.5 and what to do about each one. How codes are built # A code is a letter followed by four digits. Part Meaning First letter E is an error. X is an error after Optics tried every fallback or caught an exception. W is a warning. First two digits The family: 01 driver, 02 elements, 03 screenshots, 04 keywords, 05 files and config, 06 engines and modules, 07 test cases and variables, 08 general, 09 optics live . Last two digits The specific problem in that family. Codes in the E02 family and X0201 mean "element not found". When a step uses an element with fallback values, only these codes make Optics try the next value. Any other code fails the step straight away. Where codes appear # Where What it looks like optics execute "Failure details" box <test> → step '<step>' — Keyword '<keyword>' failed: Code.E0401: <message> Log files ( file_log: true ) The same reason as the Failure details box, as an error line in execution_logs.log . optics live history ✗ press_element ${sign_in} with [E0201] ... on the line below HTTP API ( optics serve ) A code field in the error body, or the code inside a detail string. See HTTP API . MCP server ( optics mcp ) [Code.E0106] Driver session is no longer active ... in the tool error. See MCP server . In some places the code has a Code. prefix, as in Code.E0102 . It's the same code. Search for the five characters, for example E0102 . Not every failure has a code. See Messages without a code . E01: Driver and session # Code What happened What to do E0101 Driver not initialized. A keyword ran before the driver session started. In optics live this happens when the automatic launch_app failed. Start with Launch App . In optics live , run launch_app again and read its error first. E0102 Failed to start session. The driver couldn't create a session. The Appium server refused it, Playwright couldn't open the browser, or the request took longer than 15 seconds. Check that the server is running and the device is connected with optics doctor <folder> . Check the capabilities, especially appPackage , appActivity or bundleId . Read the Appium server's own log for the cause. E0104 Driver config incomplete. A required driver setting is missing or wrong: empty Appium capabilities , no platformName , an unsupported platformName , or no server url . Fill in the driver settings in config.yaml . platformName must be Android , iOS , TizenTV or LGTV . E0105 Keyword not supported on this device platform. You used a touch or typing keyword on a Samsung or LG TV, where Appium has no touch screen. Navigate with Press Keycode and remote keys such as UP , DOWN and ENTER . See Test TV apps . E0106 Driver session is no longer active. The Appium or Selenium server dropped the session, for example after a timeout, a device disconnect or a server restart. Optics doesn't reconnect. Run the tests again. Over HTTP or MCP, end the session and start a new one. If it keeps happening, raise newCommandTimeout in the capabilities. E02: Elements # Code What happened What to do E0201 Element not found. No strategy found the element on the current screen. Also raised when a ${name} variable isn't defined, when OCR is needed but no text_detection engine is enabled, or when Scroll Until Element Appears or Swipe Until Element Appears time out. Check the locator against the screen with optics live or the page source. Put Assert Presence before the step if the element appears late, since actions don't wait. Add fallback values in Element_ID_* columns. Enable easyocr if you locate by visible text. X0201 Element not found after all fallbacks. Optics found the element, or tried every fallback value, but the action failed each time. The element may be hidden, covered, disabled, or the wrong match. Use index to pick the right match, an area of interest to

h: Ask a question or report a bug
d: Find the answer to a problem yourself, or report it so someone else can.
x: Most problems have a known fix. Start with the pages below, and ask on GitHub when they don't cover your case. Troubleshooting Fixes for common install, setup and run problems, listed by the message you see. FAQ Short answers about what Optics does, what it doesn't, and why. Glossary Every term the docs use, in one place. Where to look first # Run optics doctor on your project before anything else. It checks Python, every engine, the Appium server, connected devices and your config.yaml , and prints the fix next to each problem: $ optics doctor my-project Always pass the project folder. Without it, doctor checks your machine but not your config. If doctor shows no ❌ rows and the problem remains: **Search Troubleshooting for the exact message.** Problems are listed by the words Optics prints, such as No driver enabled or Element not found . Look up the code. If the message has a code like E0201 , Error codes says what it means and what to do. **Read the FAQ ** when something works differently from what you expected. Some behavior is a known limit, not a bug. Ask a question or report a bug # Open an issue on GitHub . Search the open and closed issues first, since someone may have hit the same problem. A good report lets someone reproduce the problem without asking you anything. Include: Your Optics version. Run optics --version . **The optics doctor output for your project.** Run optics doctor <project> and paste everything it prints. **Your config.yaml , without secrets.** Remove API keys, passwords and tokens, and replace private URLs with placeholders. The failing step. Paste the rows from modules/modules.csv and test_data/elements.csv that the step uses, and the full "Failure details" box from the run. The log. Choose the one that matches what you ran: optics execute : set file_log: true in config.yaml , run again, and attach execution_output/internal_logs.log and execution_output/execution_logs.log . Set log_level: DEBUG for the most detail. optics live : attach logs/optics_live_<time>.log from the project folder. Its path is printed when you quit. What you expected, and what happened instead. A screenshot from execution_output/ often shows the difference at a glance. Warning Logs and screenshots can contain personal data, such as names and email addresses on screen. Check them before you attach them to a public issue. Values written with the @: prefix are masked as **** in log files, but screenshots show whatever was on screen. Report a security issue # Don't open a public issue for a security problem. Report it privately, as described in the repository's security policy .

d: Fix the most common problems with installing, configuring and running Optics.
x: Problems are grouped by when they happen and named by the message Optics prints, so you can search this page for the words on your screen. Start with optics doctor <project> , which finds many of these for you. For messages with a code such as E0201 , see Error codes . Installing # optics: command not found # Your shell can't find the optics command. The installer adds it to your PATH, but only new terminals pick that up. Open a new terminal. If it still fails, add ~/.optics/bin to your PATH, as the installer printed. With pip, activate the virtual environment you installed into. Optics needs Python 3.12 or newer # Optics runs on Python 3.12 and later. pip on an older Python reports that no matching version of optics-framework exists. Check with python3 --version , then install a current Python from python.org or use the installer, which sets up its own environment. See Install Optics . "Cannot start": Optics could not load one of its dependencies # Every command stops with a red panel because a package Optics needs is missing or broken. This usually follows a partial upgrade or a package installed into the wrong environment. Run the reinstall command shown in the panel, for example pip install --force-reinstall optics-framework . It matches the way you installed Optics. optics setup refuses to install # optics setup and optics quickstart won't install engines into environments that another tool manages: Conda, pipx, uv tool , and project environments run by uv, Poetry, PDM or Pipenv. They also refuse a system Python marked as externally managed. Run the command the message suggests, such as pipx inject optics-framework … or poetry add … . Or install Optics into a plain virtual environment, where optics setup works. See Where installs are refused . EasyOCR fails under Conda # EasyOCR and Optics need different major versions of NumPy under Conda, so they can't share a Conda environment. Use the installer or a standard venv instead of Conda. The MCP server isn't installed by optics setup # optics setup --install mcp reports Invalid engine(s): mcp , and the all bundle leaves the MCP server out. Install it with pip: pip install "optics-framework[mcp]" . See MCP server . Setting up a project # "No driver enabled in …/config.yaml" # No entry under driver_sources has enabled: true . Optics also prints this when it couldn't read config.yaml at all, for example because of a YAML syntax error or a value of the wrong type, and fell back to defaults. Run optics doctor <project> . Its config: file row shows whether the file parses. Set enabled: true on one driver, or run optics configure <project> to write a working config. Check indentation: each engine is a list item, as in - appium: followed by its settings indented below. "Missing required files in …: test_cases, modules" # Optics finds files by their header row, not their names, and found no test cases file or no modules file. Check that the first line of each file is exactly right: test_case,test_step for test cases and module_name,module_step,param_1,… for modules. A spreadsheet app can add an invisible character to the first cell when it saves as "CSV UTF-8", so save as plain CSV. See How Optics finds your files . "Cannot start" panel: "No Appium server reachable at …" # Before a run, optics execute checks that the Appium server answers at the url in config.yaml . Nothing is listening there. Start the server in another terminal with appium , then run again. If the server runs on another port or machine, fix url under driver_sources . On Android, the same panel appears when adb isn't installed or no device is connected; check with adb devices . "Cannot start" panel for Selenium # No Selenium server answers at the url in config.yaml . Start one, for example with Docker: docker run -d -p 4444:4444 selenium/standalone-chrome . Check that url in config.yaml points to it, usually http://localhost:4444/wd/hub . "Selenium capabilities not found in config" # The Selenium driver needs a brow

d: Learn what Optics can and can't do, with short answers to the questions people ask most.
x: Short answers, with links to the pages that explain each one in full. These docs describe Optics 1.10.5. About Optics # Is Optics free and open source? # Yes. Optics is open source under the Apache 2.0 license, and the code is on GitHub . There's no paid edition, account or license key. Does Optics send my data anywhere? # No, not by default. Optics has no telemetry and needs no account. Tests, screenshots and results stay on your machine or CI runner. Data leaves your machine only through features you turn on: Gemini , used by plain-English mode and AI self-heal , sends screenshots and the screen's UI tree to Google. Google Cloud Vision OCR sends screenshots to Google. EasyOCR and Tesseract run locally. Remote OCR and image engines ( remote_ocr , remote_oir ) send screenshots to the URL you configure. Event reporting sends the events you label with event_name to the eventUrl in your event_attributes_json file, if you set one up. With the MCP server , Optics itself calls no AI service. Your agent's client sends what it reads to whichever model it uses. What can I test, and where does it run? # Optics tests Android and iOS apps through Appium, websites through Playwright or Selenium, and Android TV, Samsung Tizen and LG webOS apps through Appium. It can also drive locked-down production devices as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, with a camera watching the screen. Optics itself runs on macOS, Linux and Windows with Python 3.12 or newer. Testing iOS apps needs a Mac with Xcode. See Platforms . Do I need to know how to code? # No. Tests are rows in CSV or YAML files: a keyword such as Press Element and the values it needs. You can record them by running steps against the live app, or write them in a spreadsheet. You'll edit a YAML settings file and use a terminal, but you won't write code. Python and Robot Framework are there if you want them. What is Optics not good for? # Optics tests what a person does through the interface. Use other tools for unit tests, load testing, API-only contract tests and pixel-by-pixel visual comparison. Creating tests # Should I use CSV or YAML? # Use CSV unless you have a reason not to. CSV opens in any spreadsheet app, and optics live saves recordings as CSV. Use YAML when you want a whole suite in one text file that reads well in code review. Both do the same things, and you can mix them in one project. Error definitions are CSV only. See Write tests in YAML . Can people who aren't developers write tests? # Yes. That's what the file format is for. A tester can record a flow in optics live and save it, then edit the CSV files in a spreadsheet. Someone comfortable with a terminal and YAML should set up config.yaml once; after that, most work happens in the CSV files. Can I import tests from Selenium IDE, Appium or another tool? # No. Optics has no importer. Rebuild the flows by recording them, or ask an AI agent to explore the app and write the suite through the MCP server . Going the other way works: optics generate turns a suite into pytest or Robot Framework code. It skips flow-control keywords such as Run Loop and Condition , so check the output. Can AI write my tests? # Yes, two ways. Describe a flow in plain English inside optics live , and Gemini drives the app and records the steps. Or connect your AI agent through MCP and let it explore the app and write the files. Both produce ordinary CSV that you review before you rely on it. Running tests # Can I run tests in parallel? # Not within one run. optics execute runs test cases one after another on one device or browser. To test several devices at once, start a separate optics execute process for each one, each with its own project folder and config.yaml . Separate folders keep their results apart in each project's execution_output/ . See Run the same suite on different devices . How do I run only one test? # There's no command-line flag for it. List the test cases to run under include: in config.yaml , or the ones to skip under exclude: : con

d: Learn the terms used across the Optics docs.
x: Terms are listed alphabetically. Each entry links to the page that explains it in full. A # AOI (area of interest) # An AOI, or area of interest, is a rectangle that limits where Optics looks for an element, given as percentages of the screen from 0 to 100. Use it when the same text or icon appears in several places. See Search part of the screen . Appium # Appium is the open-source automation server Optics uses to drive Android, iOS and TV apps. You run the Appium server yourself, and Optics connects to it at the url in config.yaml . See Drivers . B # BLE driver # The BLE driver makes Optics act as a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard, for devices that allow no automation software. A camera watches the screen, and Optics finds elements with OCR and image matching. See Production devices . C # Capabilities # Capabilities are the settings Optics passes to a driver when it starts a session, such as the device name, the app to open or the browser to use. They go under capabilities for each driver in config.yaml . See driver_sources . config.yaml # config.yaml is the settings file in each project. It says which driver to use, how to look at the screen, and how to log and report. See config.yaml . CSV # CSV (comma-separated values) is the plain-text table format most Optics suites use, one row per step. Any spreadsheet app or text editor can open it. See Choose CSV or YAML . D # Driver # A driver is the engine that controls the target: Appium for phones and TVs, Playwright or Selenium for browsers, or the BLE driver for locked-down devices. You enable one under driver_sources in config.yaml . See Drivers . Dry run # A dry run, started with optics dry_run , checks a project for unknown keywords, missing modules and undefined variables without tapping or typing anything. Run one before every commit. See optics dry_run . E # Element # An element is a name for something on screen, such as sign_in , plus one or more values that tell Optics how to find it. Steps refer to it as ${sign_in} . See Define elements . Element source # An element source is a way for Optics to look at the screen: ask the app for an element, read its UI tree, or take a screenshot. Each driver has its own, listed under elements_sources in config.yaml . See Element sources . Elements file # An elements file is a CSV whose header starts with Element_Name,Element_ID , listing each element's name and values. The project template keeps it in test_data/elements.csv . See Elements . Engine # An engine is an optional add-on that gives Optics a capability: a driver, an element source, an OCR engine, image matching or an AI model. You install engines with optics setup and turn them on in config.yaml . See Engines and extras . Error definition # An error definition is a row in a CSV that names a message your app shows when something goes wrong, such as "Something went wrong". At the end of a run, Optics checks the last screen for these messages and reports any it finds. See Catch error screens . Execution output # The execution output is the execution_output/ folder in a project, where each run writes its JUnit report, screenshots and logs. See Outputs . Extra # An extra is the pip name for an optional engine, such as appium , easyocr or llm , installed with optics setup --install <name> or pip install "optics-framework[<name>]" . Bundles such as web and all install several at once. See Engines and extras . F # Fallback # A fallback is a second (or third) value for an element that Optics tries when the first one isn't found. For example, an element can have an XPath, then its text, then an image. See How Optics finds elements . I # Image detection # Image detection finds an element by matching a small picture of it, called a template, against a screenshot. Turn it on with templatematch under image_detection in config.yaml . See Turn on image matching . Include and exclude # Include and exclude are config.yaml lists that pick which test cases a run includes or skips, by name. Optics
